```yaml
# GitHub Actions, after the deploy step
      - name: Notify Slack
        if: always()
        run: |
          STATUS=${{ job.status == 'success' && '✅ deployed' || '❌ FAILED, rolled back' }}
          curl -s -X POST "${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL }}" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
            -d "{\"text\":\"*myapp* $STATUS · ${{ github.ref_name }} by ${{ github.actor }}\"}"
```

```yaml
# GitLab CI
deploy:
  script:
    - ssh cipi@$SERVER_HOST "sudo cipi deploy myapp" && R="✅ deployed" || R="❌ FAILED"
    - curl -s "https://api.telegram.org/bot${TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}/sendMessage" -d chat_id="$TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID" -d text="myapp $R on $CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME"
    - '[ "$R" = "✅ deployed" ] || (ssh cipi@$SERVER_HOST "sudo cipi deploy myapp --rollback"; exit 1)'
```

> [!tip] Telegram chat ID: add the bot to the group, open `https://api.telegram.org/bot/getUpdates` and read `chat.id`.


## Domains & aliases

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/domains

An app has one **primary domain** and any number of **aliases**. One certificate covers them all.

```bash
$ cipi domains            # every domain of every app, in one table
```

| Column | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| DOMAIN, APP, KIND | The name, its app, `primary` or `alias` |
| TYPE, PHP, DOCROOT, BRANCH | How the app is served and deployed |
| LAST DEPLOY | When the live release was published |
| SSL | `✓`/`✗` per name |
| suffix | `⏸ suspended` for suspended apps |

To rename the primary domain: `cipi app edit myapp --domain=new.example.com` ([Manage apps](https://cipi.sh/docs/manage-apps#edit)).

## Aliases 

```bash
$ cipi alias add myapp www.myapp.com
$ cipi alias add myapp myapp.it
$ cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com'     # wildcard: quote it
$ cipi alias list myapp
$ cipi alias remove myapp myapp.it
```

The vhost keeps serving HTTPS while you change aliases. `alias add` tells you whether the new name is already covered by the certificate or which command adds it (usually `cipi ssl install myapp`; for a wildcard `--dns=cloudflare`, see [Wildcard domains](https://cipi.sh/docs/wildcard-domains)).

## www and apex 

Pick one canonical host and 301 the other to it. Search engines see one site, and the certificate covers both.

```bash
$ cipi www force-to-root myapp      # www.myapp.com → myapp.com
$ cipi www force-from-root myapp    # myapp.com → www.myapp.com
$ cipi www status myapp
$ cipi www clear myapp
```

The missing counterpart is added as an alias automatically. ACME challenges stay reachable, so renewals keep working. In [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml#cli-yml-routes): `app.www: to-root`.

## In the web panel 

Aliases, certificates and www/apex redirects, from the browser. The [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) is optional; everything here also works from the CLI.


## SSL certificates

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl

Free Let's Encrypt certificates for every app, renewed automatically. One command covers the primary domain and every alias.

## Commands 

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi ssl install myapp` | Issue or reissue (all names in one certificate); forces HTTPS; sets `APP_URL` |
| `cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare` | Issue through Cloudflare DNS: wildcards, proxy on, no port 80 needed |
| `cipi ssl install myapp --http` | Back to HTTP validation |
| `cipi ssl force myapp` | Re-apply the HTTP → HTTPS redirect without reissuing |
| `cipi ssl status` | Certificates, expiry, and per app the names not covered |
| `cipi ssl renew` | Force renewal of everything |

## Two ways to validate 

| | HTTP-01 (default) | DNS-01 via Cloudflare |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Needs | DNS pointing at the server, port 80 open | A Cloudflare API token (Zone → DNS → Edit) |
| Wildcards | No | Yes |
| Behind Cloudflare proxy | Depends on Cloudflare rules | Always works |
| Renewal | Automatic | Automatic, with the same token |

```bash
$ cipi ssl dns set --token=CF_TOKEN
$ cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare [--wildcard]
```

A certificate is always renewed the way it was issued, and Nginx reloads after each renewal (twice-daily timer plus a weekly safety cron). Cipi writes the HTTPS block itself, so aliases, redirects, Octane, Reverb, basic auth or suspension never drop HTTPS.

## Several Cloudflare accounts 

Hosting clients with their own Cloudflare accounts? Give each token a name:

```bash
$ cipi ssl dns set --name=client-a --token=TOKEN_A
$ cipi ssl install shop --dns=cloudflare --account=client-a
$ cipi ssl dns list           # accounts and what renews with each (tokens never shown)
$ cipi ssl dns remove client-a
```

Tokens are root-only files in `/etc/cipi/cloudflare/`. Removing an account is refused while a certificate still renews with it, so nothing expires silently.

> [!warning] Behind the Cloudflare proxy set SSL/TLS to **Full (strict)**. *Flexible* creates a redirect loop with Cipi's HTTPS redirect. With [Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust) tunnels, Cloudflare terminates HTTPS and Cipi adapts automatically.


## Wildcard domains

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/wildcard-domains

One app answering on every `.myapp.com`, with one certificate for all of them. It takes two separate things:

| Part | How | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Routing** | `cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com'` (or a wildcard primary) | Works with any DNS |
| **Certificate** | `cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare` | Let's Encrypt issues wildcards over DNS only; Cipi automates Cloudflare |

## Which setup is yours 

| Your DNS | Certificate | Cloudflare SSL/TLS mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloudflare, proxied (orange) — best for SaaS | Let's Encrypt via DNS-01, or Cloudflare Origin CA | **Full (strict)** |
| Cloudflare, DNS only (grey) | Let's Encrypt via DNS-01 | not used |
| Another provider | Move DNS to Cloudflare (free), list the subdomains, or bring your own certificate | — |
| Cloudflare Tunnel ([cipi zt](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust)) | Not needed: Cloudflare terminates HTTPS | set by the tunnel |

## With Cloudflare, step by step 

```flow
DNS records | A @ and A * → server
API token | Zone → DNS → Edit
Wildcard alias | routes subdomains
Certificate | DNS-01, ~1 minute
Full (strict) | if proxied
```

```bash
$ cipi ssl dns set --token=YOUR_CLOUDFLARE_TOKEN
$ cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com'
$ cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare
$ cipi ssl status
$ curl -sI https://tenant1.myapp.com | head -1
```

The token needs only **Zone → DNS → Edit** on that zone. Renewals happen by themselves with the same token. `--wildcard` adds `myapp.com` + `*.myapp.com` to the certificate even without a wildcard alias (handy for many explicit subdomains); it does not route anything.

## Cloudflare errors decoded 

| You see | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` | SSL/TLS mode Flexible (globally or in a rule) | Full (strict) |
| 525 SSL handshake failed | No app has that hostname, or it has no certificate yet | Add the alias / issue the certificate |
| 526 Invalid SSL certificate | The certificate doesn't cover the hostname | `cipi ssl status`, then reissue |
| Deep names fail (`a.b.myapp.com`) | Universal SSL covers one level | Keep tenants one label deep |

## Without Cloudflare 

| Option | When |
| --- | --- |
| Move DNS to Cloudflare, records "DNS only" | Recommended: free, traffic unchanged |
| List each subdomain as an alias, HTTP-01 | Few, known tenants (max 100 names per certificate) |
| Bring your own certificate with your provider's certbot plugin | Route 53, DigitalOcean, OVH, Gandi… |

```bash
# bring your own: name the certificate after the app's primary domain
$ apt install python3-certbot-dns-route53
$ certbot certonly --dns-route53 -d myapp.com -d '*.myapp.com' --cert-name myapp.com
$ cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com'    # Cipi finds and serves it
```

Don't run `cipi ssl install` on that app afterwards: it would reissue over HTTP without the wildcard.

## Multi-tenant tips 

- **Exact names win**: with `*.myapp.com` on one app, `api.myapp.com` can still be another app.
- **Unknown hosts are closed** by the [default server](https://cipi.sh/docs/nginx#cli-nginx), not sent to your tenant resolver.
- **Laravel**: resolve the tenant from the `Host` header; set `SESSION_DOMAIN=.myapp.com` only to share logins across subdomains.
- **Need isolation per tenant** (own database, backups, server)? Create one Cipi app per tenant through the [API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) instead.


## Redirects & proxies

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/redirects-proxies

Move pages or whole sites without losing visitors or search ranking, and route a path to another service. Rules live in Cipi's state and survive every vhost change.

## Redirect a whole app 

Every name the app answers to (primary, aliases, www) goes to the target in **one hop**.

```bash
$ cipi redirect set oldsite --to=https://new.com            # 301, path and query kept
$ cipi redirect set oldsite --to=https://new.com --302 --no-path
$ cipi redirect disable oldsite      # serve the app again, keep the target
$ cipi redirect enable oldsite
$ cipi redirect unset oldsite
```

Status codes: `--301` (default), `--302`, `--307`, `--308`. The old name's certificate keeps renewing, so HTTPS visitors get a valid redirect too.

## Redirect paths 

```bash
$ cipi redirect add myapp /old-pricing /pricing
$ cipi redirect add myapp /blog/ https://blog.example.com/
$ cipi redirect add myapp /docs/ https://docs.example.com --308 --no-path
$ cipi redirect list myapp
$ cipi redirect remove myapp /old-pricing
```

| `from` | Matches | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/old` (no trailing slash) | Exactly that path; query kept | `/old?x=1` → `/new?x=1` |
| `/blog/` (trailing slash) | The prefix; the rest is appended | `/blog/x?y` → `https://blog.example.com/x?y` |
| with `--no-path` | Everything to the target as is | `/blog/x` → `https://blog.example.com/` |

Path redirects and proxies keep working while an app redirect is on, so a moved site can keep `/api/` in place.

## Proxy a path to another service 

Hand `/api/`, `/events/` or `/docs/` to a Node or Go service, a legacy app or another origin.

```bash
$ cipi proxy add myapp /api/ http://127.0.0.1:3000 --strip-prefix
$ cipi proxy add myapp /events/ http://127.0.0.1:4000 --no-buffering --timeout=3600
$ cipi proxy add myapp /docs/ https://docs-origin.example.com --preserve-host
$ cipi proxy list myapp
$ cipi proxy remove myapp /api/
```

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| (none) | URI unchanged: `/api/users` → `upstream/api/users` |
| `--strip-prefix` | `/api/users` → `upstream/users`, with `X-Forwarded-Prefix` |
| `--preserve-host` | Send the visitor's `Host` |
| `--timeout=N` | Upstream timeout in seconds |
| `--no-buffering` | For Server-Sent Events, long polling, streaming |

Every proxy carries WebSocket upgrade and `X-Real-IP` / `X-Forwarded-*` headers; basic auth, when on, covers it too.

## Safety rails 

| Guard | Protects against |
| --- | --- |
| Strict charset for paths and URLs | Injecting Nginx directives |
| Reserved paths (`/`, ACME, `/robots.txt`, `/cipi/webhook`, Reverb's `/app`) | Breaking certificates, webhooks or WebSockets |
| Loop and overlap detection | Redirect loops; a redirect and a proxy on the same prefix |
| Loopback guard | Proxying to Cipi's own ports (SSH, databases, Valkey, Octane, Reverb) without `--force`; the panel and cipi.yml can never force |
| `nginx -t` before reload | A bad rule: config and state are restored, exit code 1 |

Changes fire `redirect_change` / `proxy_change` [notifications](https://cipi.sh/docs/notifications). Also available in the panel, the API and [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml#cli-yml-routes).


## Nginx

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/nginx

Cipi runs Nginx from nginx.org's mainline repository, hardened and kept patched. This page covers the security report, upgrades and the default server.

## Security report 

```bash
$ cipi nginx security
```

| Reports | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Installed version vs. the oldest with every known fix | Are you exposed to a published CVE? |
| Whether the running binary is the one on disk | An upgrade isn't real until the old workers are gone |
| Every config file that turns HTTP/2 on | Most recent HTTP/2 CVEs need it |

Cipi's vhosts use `listen 443 ssl;` and never enable HTTP/2, which removes a whole class of vulnerabilities from a standard Cipi server. [How Cipi handled the nginx 1.31.9 CVEs](https://cipi.sh/guides/php-nginx-cve-patching) walks through a real case.

## Upgrades 

Nginx is excluded from unattended upgrades so it never restarts unexpectedly. Patch it on your terms:

```bash
$ cipi nginx upgrade [--yes]      # now
$ cipi autoupdate on nginx        # or nightly, automatically
```

```flow
apt upgrade nginx | your nginx.conf kept
nginx -t | must pass
Reload | graceful
Check binary | restart if old workers linger
```

If a long-lived connection (a WebSocket) keeps an old worker on the replaced binary, Cipi restarts Nginx instead of reloading (well under a second of interruption). A server found on Ubuntu's archive Nginx is moved to nginx.org mainline in one simulated-first transaction: if anything can't be done, nothing changes.

## Default server 

```bash
$ cipi nginx default-server status|on|off
```

On by default: requests for unknown hostnames, on HTTP and HTTPS, get an empty reply (444) instead of reaching one of your apps or a tenant resolver.

## Custom Nginx config 

Cipi generates each vhost (`/etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp`) and regenerates it when you change aliases, PHP, SSL, redirects or proxies. Prefer Cipi's commands and [cipi.yml routes](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml#cli-yml-routes) over hand edits; if you must edit, test and reload:

```bash
$ sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp
$ sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx
```

> [!warning] Hand edits are overwritten by the next regeneration. Keep them small and documented, and re-check with `cipi nginx security`.


## PHP versions & php.ini

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/php

Run several PHP versions side by side, give each app its own, and keep all of them patched. Cipi installs from packages.sury.org (fastest with security releases), then the ondrej PPA, then Ubuntu.

## Versions 

```bash
$ cipi php list                # versions, patch level, security state, default
$ cipi php install 8.4         # add a version (8.3–8.6)
$ cipi php switch 8.6          # server default (CLI, panel pools)
$ cipi php remove 8.1          # refused while it's the default or an app uses it
$ cipi app edit myapp --php=8.6  # move one app, zero downtime
```

| Version | Status on Cipi |
| --- | --- |
| 8.6 | Default on new servers once the repository has every extension Cipi needs |
| 8.3, 8.4, 8.5 | Installable and assignable |
| 7.4–8.2 (old servers) | Listed, restartable, removable; never offered to an app |

Each app's deploys, Composer, cron and workers always use **the app's** PHP, never the server default.

## A new PHP minor 

When a new minor comes out, the extension packages (`redis`, `memcached`, `imagick`) follow a few days later. Cipi handles the gap:

| Situation | Cipi |
| --- | --- |
| PHP packaged, some extensions not yet | Installs it, records what's missing, adds each extension as soon as it's published (nightly) |
| Only a release candidate available | Installs it and labels it **prerelease** |
| Assigning a version still missing extensions | Refused with the list of what's missing; `--force` if the app doesn't use them |
| A lock file that rejects the new PHP | The deploy fails and the live release stays: update the dependency, commit, deploy |

## Security patches 

PHP is excluded from Ubuntu's unattended upgrades: Cipi patches it itself **every night at 03:30**, restarts only the affected PHP-FPM services and reports the result.

```bash
$ cipi php upgrade      # patch now and print the patch level
```

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `patched` | At or past the latest security release Cipi knows |
| `VULNERABLE` | A fix exists but isn't installed yet (exit code 1; the nightly job alerts until fixed) |
| `distro` | Ubuntu build: fixes backported without a version bump |
| `END OF LIFE` | No more fixes from PHP: move apps off it |
| `prerelease` | Release candidate, not compared |

[Octane](https://cipi.sh/docs/octane) apps run the PHP inside their FrankenPHP binary, which apt never touches; `cipi php upgrade` lists them too and `cipi frankenphp upgrade` fixes them.

## Hardening 

Every pool Cipi writes (apps, webhook receivers, panel) locks down settings that recent PHP advisories used as attack paths, and Octane apps load the same rules:

```ini
php_admin_flag[session.upload_progress.enabled] = off
php_admin_flag[fatal_error_backtraces] = off
```

They are set as admin flags, so neither `.user.ini` nor `ini_set()` can turn them back on. Vhosts never enable `fastcgi_keep_conn`. Real-world walkthrough: [How Cipi handles PHP and nginx CVEs](https://cipi.sh/guides/php-nginx-cve-patching).

## php.ini settings: `cipi ini` 

Change PHP settings without hunting for the right file. Server-wide changes reach **PHP-FPM and CLI**, so web requests, workers, Artisan and cron agree.

```bash
$ cipi ini list [--app=shop]                  # effective values and where each comes from
$ cipi ini set upload_max_filesize=50M        # server-wide
$ cipi ini set memory_limit=512M --app=shop   # one app only (wins)
$ cipi ini unset memory_limit --app=shop
$ cipi ini reset [--app=shop]
$ cipi ini keys                               # what can and can't be set
```

| Behaviour | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Raising `upload_max_filesize` raises `post_max_size`/`memory_limit` if they'd cap it | One command, a working upload limit |
| Nginx `client_max_body_size` flagged when it would cap it | No mystery 413 errors |
| `open_basedir`, `auto_prepend_file`, `extension`… refused | They are part of app isolation |
| Every change fires the `ini_set` notification | Nothing changes on a shared server without a trace |

Per-app settings can also live in [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml) as `app.ini`.


## Node.js

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/nodejs

Official Node.js builds for [Node apps](https://cipi.sh/docs/node-apps) and for Laravel asset builds. Every download is verified against nodejs.org's `SHASUMS256.txt`; only even (LTS) majors are offered.

```bash
$ cipi node install 24            # x64 or arm64, checksum-verified
$ cipi node list                  # majors, default, apps on each
$ cipi node upgrade 22 --restart  # latest patch; SSR apps restart blue/green
$ cipi node default 22            # server-wide Node for builds, app run, deploy.post
$ cipi node default system        # back to the distribution package
$ cipi node remove 20             # refused while in use
```

| Layer | Picks the Node used by |
| --- | --- |
| Server default (`cipi node default`) | Laravel `--node-build`, `cipi app run … npm`, `deploy.post`, new Node apps |
| Per Laravel app (`cipi app edit myapp --node-version=24`) | That app's builds only |
| Per Node app (`--node-version`) | That app's runtime |

Runtimes live in `/opt/cipi/node/` behind an atomic symlink per major, so `cipi node upgrade` moves every app on that major at once. Files you installed yourself in `/usr/local/bin` are never overwritten. The panel can list runtimes and restart Node apps; installing software stays a root-only CLI action.


## Databases

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/databases

Each Laravel app gets its own database and user, so no app can read another's data. MariaDB is the default; PostgreSQL can be added and chosen per app or per database.

## Engines 

```bash
$ cipi db install pgsql             # add PostgreSQL next to MariaDB
$ cipi db default mariadb|pgsql     # default when --engine is omitted
$ cipi db engines
$ cipi db uninstall pgsql           # destroys its data: asks first
```

| | MariaDB | PostgreSQL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Port | 3306 (localhost) | 5432 (localhost) |
| Installed | Always | `cipi db install pgsql` |
| Laravel `DB_CONNECTION` | `mysql` | `pgsql` |
| Why choose it | [Design decisions](https://cipi.sh/docs/design-decisions#why-mariadb) | [Design decisions](https://cipi.sh/docs/design-decisions#why-postgresql) |

## Databases 

```bash
$ cipi db create --name=analytics --engine=pgsql
$ cipi db create --name=wpblog --app=blog     # belongs to the "blog" app
$ cipi db link wpblog blog                    # or link an existing one
$ cipi db list [--json]                       # sizes and owning app
$ cipi db backup myapp
$ cipi db restore myapp backup.sql.gz
$ cipi db password myapp                      # new password, .env updated
$ cipi db delete analytics
```

Each database has its own user and password. Linking is a label: a linked database is listed with its app (in the CLI and the panel) and is **kept** when the app is deleted; only a Laravel app's own database goes with it. Connect from TablePlus or DBeaver with the `mariadb+ssh://` URL shown at creation: no database port is ever exposed.

## Restores you can trust 

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Stops at the first failing statement | Clear error, exit 1, no "restored" lie |
| PostgreSQL restore in one transaction | A truncated or failing dump rolls back; your data stays |
| Empty dumps refused | A backup of nothing never wipes a database |
| Newer `pg_dump` into older server | Unknown `SET` lines are dropped so it still restores |
| Files from an app's home opened as that user | A malicious symlink can't make root read other files |

## Upgrades 

Database engines are excluded from unattended upgrades, so they never restart under you. Patch when you choose (brief restart):

```bash
$ cipi db upgrade [mariadb|pgsql] [--yes]
```

Or schedule it with [cipi autoupdate](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades).

## In the web panel 

Every database on every server, with backup, restore and password rotation. The [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) is optional; everything here also works from the CLI.


## Valkey

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/valkey

Valkey is the open-source (BSD, Linux Foundation) continuation of Redis: same protocol, same `phpredis` driver, same `REDIS_*` variables. Cipi gives **each Laravel app its own instance**, so no app can read or flush another's cache, sessions or jobs.

| Per-app instance | |
| --- | --- |
| Service | `cipi-valkey@myapp`, running as the app's user |
| Network | `127.0.0.1`, its own port (from 6400) and password |
| Config / data | `/etc/cipi-valkey/myapp.conf`, `/var/lib/cipi-valkey/myapp` |
| Cost | About 10 MB of RAM when idle |
| `.env` | `REDIS_HOST`, `REDIS_PORT`, `REDIS_PASSWORD` already written |

## Use it in Laravel 

New apps keep cache, sessions and queues in their database. Switch whatever you want to Valkey:

```bash
$ cipi app env myapp --set=CACHE_STORE=redis
$ cipi app env myapp --set=SESSION_DRIVER=redis
$ cipi app env myapp --set=QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis
$ cipi worker restart myapp            # or enable Horizon
```

## Manage instances 

```bash
$ cipi valkey list
$ cipi valkey isolate shop                     # move an app off the shared instance
$ cipi valkey isolate --all
$ cipi valkey isolate shop --maxmemory=256mb --policy=allkeys-lru
$ cipi valkey restart shop
$ cipi valkey flush-shared                     # once no app uses it: empty + new password
```

```flow
Maintenance on | app returns 503
Workers stop | nothing writes
Copy keys | with their expiry
Switch .env | config cache rebuilt
Back online | seconds later
```

If the copy fails, the app stays exactly where it was. Apps whose Redis points elsewhere are left alone. Clones and synced apps get their own instance. `cipi pending` lists apps still on the shared instance.

> [!note] `cipi app create --valkey=shared` keeps one app on the server-wide instance. Valkey is excluded from unattended upgrades; patch it with [stack upgrades](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades).


## Search (Meilisearch)

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/search

Full-text search for Laravel Scout, self-hosted: no Algolia account, no per-record billing. Meilisearch runs natively (a single binary with systemd), listens on localhost only, and every app gets a key that can touch **its own indexes and nothing else**. Off until you install it.

```bash
$ cipi search install             # binary, config, hardened unit; checks /health
$ cipi search enable myapp        # scoped key + SCOUT_* in .env
$ cipi app artisan myapp scout:import "App\Models\Product"
$ cipi search status [--check]
$ cipi search disable myapp [--purge-indexes]
```

Step-by-step with a real model: [Laravel Scout with Meilisearch on Cipi](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-scout-meilisearch).

> [!tip] Small dataset? Scout's `database` driver or PostgreSQL full-text need no extra service. `cipi search status` says so on servers without Meilisearch.

## Isolation by design 

```flow
App myapp | SCOUT_PREFIX=myapp-
Scoped key | indexes myapp-* only
Meilisearch | 127.0.0.1, no public port
```

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Prefix written by Cipi, not chosen by you | App names can't overlap, so prefixes can't either |
| Key limited to Scout's actions on `myapp-*` | No key management, no other app's indexes (a stray index name gets 403) |
| Master key in a root-only file, never on a command line | App users can't read it from `/proc` |
| Delete or clone an app | Its key is revoked / the clone gets a new key and prefix, never production's |
| Memory check before install | Refused below 512 MB available, warned below 1 GB |

## Commands 

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi search list` | Apps with search and their prefixes |
| `cipi search key show\|rotate myapp` | Show or replace an app's key (`.env` updated) |
| `cipi search key rotate --master` | New master key; every app's `.env` is rewritten in the same run |
| `cipi search upgrade [--version=]` | Upgrade in place; the old binary returns if the store is refused |
| `cipi search remove [--keep-data]` | Uninstall |

The panel can show status and enable/disable search per app; installing, upgrading, rotating and removing stay on the CLI.


## Services

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/services

See and control every service Cipi runs. Nginx always reloads gracefully, so restarting it never drops a request.

```bash
$ cipi service list [nginx] [--json]
$ cipi service restart              # everything
$ cipi service restart nginx        # graceful reload
$ cipi service restart php          # every PHP-FPM version
$ cipi service start fail2ban
$ cipi service stop supervisor      # asks first
$ cipi service upgrade              # installed vs available versions
$ cipi service upgrade valkey [--yes]
```

| Name | Service |
| --- | --- |
| `nginx` | Web server |
| `php` or `php8.6-fpm` | All PHP-FPM versions, or one |
| `mariadb`, `postgresql` (`pgsql`) | Databases |
| `valkey-server` (`redis`, `valkey`) | Shared Valkey |
| `supervisor` | Workers, Octane, Horizon, Reverb |
| `fail2ban` | Brute-force protection |
| `meilisearch` (`search`), `cloudflared` | Only when installed |

`upgrade all` is refused on purpose: patch one service at a time and watch it come back. REST: `GET /api/services`, `POST /api/services/{name}/restart`.


## Packages

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/packages

Tools some Laravel packages need on the host, from Ubuntu's own repositories, through a **closed allowlist**: never a root apt shell. Nothing is installed until you ask.

```bash
$ cipi package list
$ cipi package install image-optimizers
$ cipi package install ffmpeg
$ cipi package install webp            # one binary from a group
$ cipi package remove ffmpeg
```

| Package | Installs | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `image-optimizers` | jpegoptim, optipng, pngquant, gifsicle, webp | `spatie/laravel-image-optimizer` |
| `ffmpeg` | ffmpeg | `pbmedia/laravel-ffmpeg` (run it in a queue worker, never in a request) |
| `imagemagick` | `convert` / `magick` CLI | Code that shells out to ImageMagick (the PHP extension is already installed) |
| `poppler-utils` | `pdftotext` | `spatie/pdf-to-text`, feeding PDFs to search |

Install and remove show what apt will do (packages, disk space) and ask first; afterwards Cipi checks each binary is on the `PATH`. Removal previews orphaned dependencies before cleaning them up. Anything with a daemon, a port or state is a service, not a package: see [search](https://cipi.sh/docs/search) and [databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases).


## Stack upgrades

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades

Security patches for the whole stack, without surprise restarts. Ubuntu's unattended upgrades would restart Nginx or a database whenever they run; Cipi takes those packages over and patches them at a quiet hour, one at a time, checking each one.

| Component | Patched by | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ubuntu (kernel, libraries…) | unattended-upgrades | Daily |
| PHP | [cipi php upgrade](https://cipi.sh/docs/php#security) | Daily, 03:30 |
| Nginx, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Valkey, Node.js, Composer, FrankenPHP | `cipi autoupdate` | Nightly, 04:20 |
| Reboot for a new kernel | `cipi reboot auto` | Off unless you turn it on |

## Nightly patches: `cipi autoupdate` 

```bash
$ cipi autoupdate                    # what's on, how the last run went
$ cipi autoupdate off mariadb        # patch this one yourself
$ cipi autoupdate on
$ cipi autoupdate run [name]         # now
```

| Rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Patch releases only (`--only-upgrade`) | No major jumps overnight |
| Your config files are kept; `nginx -t` before reload | A patch never breaks the config |
| Node runtimes checked against SHA-256; Composer rolled back if it won't start | Verified binaries only |
| One at a time, databases last; skipped during a dump or deploy | No restart in the middle of your work |
| Octane builds stay on their PHP minor, health-checked, rolled back if silent | [FrankenPHP pinning](https://cipi.sh/docs/octane#cli-frankenphp) |
| Each upgrade notified; failures alert and show in `cipi pending` | You always know |

Log: `/var/log/cipi/autoupdate.log`.

## By hand 

```bash
$ cipi nginx upgrade [--yes]
$ cipi db upgrade [mariadb|pgsql] [--yes]
$ cipi service upgrade valkey [--yes]
$ cipi service upgrade                 # installed vs available
```

Package patterns are pinned (a loose match can't drag PHP in), vendor repositories are re-asserted if missing, and a lock prevents two upgrades from overlapping. These are not exposed to the panel: patching a database is an operator decision.

## What needs you: `cipi pending` 

A server can be fully patched and still run last month's kernel. `cipi pending` lists what an update can't do by itself, each with the command to run:

```bash
$ cipi pending [--json]
```

| Item | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Reboot required | New kernel installed, old one running |
| Below a security release | PHP, Nginx, Composer, Node.js |
| Old binary still running | Nginx upgraded on disk, workers not yet replaced |
| Updates waiting | A component with autoupdate off, or whose last run failed |
| Unmanaged code | PHP extensions built by hand or with PECL |
| App hygiene | Horizon installed but not running; apps on the shared Valkey |

Checked every morning; mailed when the list changes, and weekly while something stays on it. `cipi status` shows it too.

## Reboots 

```bash
$ cipi reboot                         # needed? since when? which kernel?
$ cipi reboot now [--yes]
$ cipi reboot auto on --at=04:45      # only on nights one is required
```

Automatic reboots notify, warn two minutes ahead, and wait for the next night while a package install, dump, deploy or other `cipi` command is running.


## Server commands & updates

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/server-commands

The everyday commands for the server itself.

| Command | Shows or does |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi status` | CPU, RAM, disk, services, PHP versions, apps, pending items |
| `cipi disk` | Disk usage of the server and each app ([Disk usage](https://cipi.sh/docs/disk)) |
| `cipi pending` | What needs a human ([Stack upgrades](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades#pending)) |
| `cipi version` | Installed Cipi version |
| `cipi help [topic]` | Every command, grouped |

## Credentials 

```bash
$ cipi credentials                       # root, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Valkey, Meilisearch, backup key
$ cipi credentials export > cipi.csv     # CSV for any password manager
$ cipi reset root-password
$ cipi reset db-password [--engine=pgsql]
$ cipi reset valkey-password             # restarts the shared Valkey
```

Run the export from your laptop (`ssh cipi@server sudo cipi credentials export > cipi.csv`) so no copy stays on the server. Every show or export is logged and notified (`credentials_show`). Secrets are stored encrypted ([Vault](https://cipi.sh/docs/vault)).

## Updating Cipi 

```bash
$ cipi self-update --check
$ cipi self-update
```

```flow
Download | from GitHub
Back up | /opt/cipi.bak.
Replace CLI | scripts and libraries
Migrations | in order, each idempotent
Done | apps untouched
```

Updates never deploy your apps or touch their code and data. Migrations bring existing servers in line with new defaults (a security setting, a new hook); each one is written to be safe to re-run and to degrade to a warning instead of breaking the update. A nightly job (03:50) applies updates automatically; run it yourself first if you'd rather watch. What changed in each release: [What's new](https://cipi.sh/whats-new) and the [changelog on GitHub](https://github.com/cipi-sh/cipi/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md).

## Tab completion 

Installed for you for bash and zsh, for root and the `cipi` user, in login and non-login shells (`su`, tmux), including after `sudo`:

```bash
$ sudo cipi dep          # → deploy
$ sudo cipi deploy sh    # → shop  shop-stg   (your apps)
$ cipi completion zsh --print # the script, for another user or rc file
```

It completes commands, sub-commands, flags, help topics and app names.


## Uninstall

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/uninstall

Cipi changes a server deeply (users, SSH, firewall, packages, repositories), so there is no `uninstall` command. **The clean way out is a fresh server**: move the apps elsewhere with [cipi sync](https://cipi.sh/docs/sync) or your backups, then destroy the VPS. The steps below exist for when you must keep the machine.

> [!warning] This deletes every app, database, certificate and configuration Cipi manages. Back up first ([Backups](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups)). It cannot be undone.

```flow
Back up | backups, credentials export
Remove apps | users, vhosts, pools, databases
Remove Cipi | users, binaries, config, cron
Purge packages | optional
Restore SSH & firewall | last
```

## 1. Apps 

```bash
$ grep cipi-apps /etc/group                     # list app users
# for each APP:
$ supervisorctl stop "APP:*"
$ rm -f /etc/supervisor/conf.d/APP.conf /etc/nginx/sites-{enabled,available}/APP \
        /etc/php/*/fpm/pool.d/APP.conf /etc/sudoers.d/cipi-APP*
$ mysql -e "DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS APP; DROP USER IF EXISTS 'APP'@'localhost';"
$ userdel -r APP
```

## 2. Cipi itself 

```bash
$ systemctl disable --now cipi-queue 2>/dev/null; rm -f /etc/systemd/system/cipi-queue.service
$ userdel -r cipi; groupdel cipi-ssh; groupdel cipi-apps
$ rm -rf /opt/cipi /etc/cipi /var/log/cipi /usr/local/bin/cipi*
$ rm -f /etc/sudoers.d/cipi-* /etc/logrotate.d/cipi-* /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/*cipi* \
        /etc/profile.d/cipi-* /etc/mysql/mariadb.conf.d/99-cipi.cnf /etc/php/*/*/conf.d/99-cipi.ini
$ crontab -e                                    # remove the Cipi block
```

## 3. Packages and repositories (optional) 

```bash
$ systemctl stop nginx mariadb valkey-server fail2ban supervisor 'php*-fpm'
$ apt purge -y 'nginx*' mariadb-server mariadb-client valkey-server fail2ban supervisor certbot 'php8.*' nodejs
$ apt autoremove -y
$ rm -f /etc/apt/sources.list.d/{php-sury,mariadb,nodesource}.list && apt update
$ rm -f /usr/local/bin/composer /usr/local/bin/dep
$ swapoff /var/swap.1 && rm -f /var/swap.1 && sed -i '/swap\.1/d' /etc/fstab
```

## 4. SSH and firewall (last) 

Do this from a console session, not over SSH, so a mistake can't lock you out:

```bash
$ sed -i '/cipi-auth-notify/d' /etc/pam.d/sshd /etc/pam.d/sudo
$ nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config        # review PermitRootLogin / PasswordAuthentication
$ systemctl restart ssh
$ ufw disable && ufw reset
```


## Backups to S3

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/backups

Backups that run on their own, go where you want, are encrypted before they leave the server, and tell you when they stop. Built on **profiles**: each one answers *what*, *how often*, *where* and *how long*.

```flow
Profile runs | on its schedule
Dump + archive | per database, per app
Integrity check | before upload
Encrypt | AES-256, on the server
Upload | local, S3, other buckets
Prune & watch | retention, staleness alert
```

## 1. Destinations 

```bash
$ cipi backup configure          # the default bucket ("s3"); leave empty for local-only
$ cipi backup destination add offsite --bucket=acme-backups --key=AKIA… --secret=… \
    --region=eu-central-1 --endpoint=https://eu-central-1.your-objectstorage.com
$ cipi backup destination test   # reach every bucket with its own credentials
$ cipi backup status [--json]    # destinations, profiles, last run, overdue, uncovered
```

| Provider | Endpoint |
| --- | --- |
| AWS S3 | leave empty |
| Cloudflare R2 | `https://.r2.cloudflarestorage.com` |
| Hetzner Object Storage | `https://.your-objectstorage.com` |
| DigitalOcean Spaces | `https://.digitaloceanspaces.com` |
| Backblaze B2 | `https://s3..backblazeb2.com` |
| Scaleway | `https://s3..scw.cloud` |
| MinIO | `https://your-minio-host` |

`local` (`/var/backups/cipi`) is always available. A profile can send each run to several destinations at once.

## 2. Profiles 

```bash
# every 30 minutes: databases only, on the server, last 48 runs
$ cipi backup profile add hourly-db --scope=db --databases='shop,tenant_*' \
    --exclude-tables='*.jobs,*.telescope_*' --every=30m --keep=48 --dest=local
# every night: files + databases, encrypted, two buckets, 14 days
$ cipi backup profile add nightly --scope=all --cron='0 2 * * *' --keep-days=14 \
    --dest=s3,offsite --encrypt
```

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--scope=all\|files\|db` | What to take |
| `--apps`, `--databases`, `--exclude-databases` | Glob patterns; tenant databases created at runtime are found too |
| `--exclude-tables` | Skip noisy tables (`*.jobs`, `*.telescope_*`) |
| `--every=30m\|6h\|1d` or `--cron='…'` | Schedule |
| `--dest=local,s3,` | Where to send it |
| `--keep=N`, `--keep-days=N`, `--keep-weeks=N` | Retention |
| `--encrypt` | AES-256 before upload |

```bash
$ cipi backup profile list | show nightly | edit nightly --keep-days=30
$ cipi backup profile disable hourly-db | enable hourly-db
$ cipi backup profile remove hourly-db [--purge]   # --purge also deletes its runs
```

Apps can declare their own profiles in [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml) (named `` or `-*`); server-wide profiles stay yours.

## 3. Encryption 

The bucket provider never sees readable data. The manifest stays readable so runs can be listed.

```bash
$ cipi backup key show       # store it off-server, now
$ cipi backup key rotate     # new key for future runs
```

> [!warning] Without the key, an encrypted backup cannot be restored by anyone. Runs taken before a rotation still need the old key.

## 4. Run, verify, restore 

```bash
$ cipi backup run [--profile=nightly] [--dry-run] [--detach]
$ cipi backup list [--profile=nightly]
$ cipi backup verify [--deep]               # does the newest run open?
$ cipi backup fetch nightly 2026-11-02_020000 --dest=/root/restore
$ cipi db restore myapp /root/restore/databases/mariadb/myapp.sql.gz
$ tar -xzf /root/restore/apps/myapp/files.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore-files
```

| Honesty check | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Archive integrity tested before upload | A dump cut short by a full disk never replaces a good backup |
| Staleness watchdog (hourly) | `backup_stale` when a profile hasn't succeeded in twice its interval |
| Empty fetch / nothing to verify | Reported as an error, never as success |
| Prune errors | Logged and alerted, never swallowed |

## Layout 

```tree
/cipi///
├── manifest.json
├── apps/myapp/files.tar.gz        # + meta.json
└── databases/mariadb/myapp.sql.gz
```

Files and databases are stored separately, so a database restores without unpacking an app. Staging uses `/var/tmp` (disk), not a small RAM-backed `/tmp`. Meilisearch indexes are not backed up: `scout:import` rebuilds them from the database.


## Server sync & migration

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/sync

Move, copy or replicate whole apps between Cipi servers: configuration, deploy keys, workers, crontab, and optionally database and storage. Archives are **encrypted with AES-256** and a passphrase, so credentials are safe at rest and in transit. Migrating providers becomes one command.

```flow
Export | encrypted archive
Transfer | rsync over SSH
Import | apps created or updated
DNS + SSL | switch when ready
```

## Commands 

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi sync export [apps] [--with-db] [--with-storage]` | Write an encrypted archive |
| `cipi sync import  [apps] [--update] [--deploy]` | Create (or update) apps from it |
| `cipi sync push [apps] --host=IP [--with-db] [--with-storage] [--import]` | Export + transfer + import in one go |
| `cipi sync list ` | Inspect an archive without importing |
| `cipi sync pubkey` / `cipi sync trust` | Key-based trust between two servers |

Add `--passphrase="$(cat /etc/cipi/.sync_passphrase)"` for scripts (store it with `chmod 400`).

## What travels 

| Item | Included |
| --- | --- |
| `.env`, `auth.json`, `deploy.php` | Always |
| Deploy key, SSH config, known hosts | Always: the same key keeps working on GitHub |
| Workers, crontab, PHP version, limits, cipi.yml auto-apply | Always |
| Database dump | `--with-db` |
| `shared/storage` | `--with-storage` |
| Certificates | Never: run `cipi ssl install` after the DNS switch |

## Import: new vs existing apps 

| | New app | Existing app (`--update`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User, directories, vhost, pool, workers | Created | Regenerated |
| Database credentials | **New** random password, written to `.env` | Target keeps its own |
| Rest of `.env` (`APP_KEY`, mail…) | From the archive | From the archive |
| Database data | Imported | Tables replaced |
| PHP version | As source (must be installed) | Migrated if it changed |

Pre-flight checks block an import that would clash with an existing app or domain. New passwords are printed once at the end.

## Recipes 

**Migrate a whole server** (e.g. AWS → Hetzner):

```bash
# on the new server: cipi sync trust (paste the key from: cipi sync pubkey on the old one)
$ cipi sync push --host=NEW_IP --with-db --with-storage --import
# on the new server, after pointing DNS:
$ cipi ssl install shop && cipi ssl install blog
```

**Warm standby every 6 hours** (data-loss window = interval):

```bash
0 */6 * * * /usr/local/bin/cipi sync push --host=STANDBY_IP --with-db --with-storage --import --passphrase="$(cat /etc/cipi/.sync_passphrase)" >> /var/log/cipi/sync.log 2>&1
```

If the primary fails: point DNS at the standby, `cipi ssl install` each app, done.

**Portable nightly archive:**

```bash
0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/cipi sync export --with-db --with-storage --output=/root/backups/cipi-$(date +\%F).tar.gz.enc --passphrase="$(cat /etc/cipi/.sync_passphrase)"
```

> [!note] Database sync is a full replace and storage a full extract (files deleted on the source remain on the target). Node apps are not synced yet. For point-in-time history use [Backups](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups).


## Health checks

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks

Two different questions, two checks: *is the site up?* and *did the release I just shipped break it?* Combined with automatic rollback, a bad deploy can undo itself within seconds.

| Check | Runs | Alerts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Periodic probe | Every 5 minutes | After 3 consecutive failures (`health_fail`) |
| Post-deploy check | Right after every release, CLI and webhook alike | Immediately (`deploy_health_fail`) |

```bash
$ cipi health set myapp --url=https://myapp.com/up --expect=200
$ cipi health check myapp
$ cipi health list [--json]
$ cipi health unset myapp
```

Laravel 11+ serves `/up` when `health: '/up'` is set in `bootstrap/app.php`. The URL must belong to the app's own domains.

## After every deploy 

```flow
Release live | symlink swapped
Grace period | 3 s, 8 s for Octane
Probe up to 5× | tolerant of warm-up
Verdict | in the deploy notice
Optional rollback | if unhealthy
```

```bash
$ cipi health set myapp --grace=15            # longer warm-up (max 120 s)
$ cipi health set myapp --no-postdeploy       # keep the 5-minute probe only
$ cipi health postdeploy myapp                # run the verification now
```

The success notification is sent **after** the verdict, so it never announces a release that returns errors. A failed verdict tells you where the check is configured and how to change it.

## Automatic rollback 

```bash
$ cipi health set myapp --rollback-on-unhealthy   # always, for this app
$ cipi deploy myapp --rollback-on-unhealthy       # this deploy only
```

| Outcome reported | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Recovered | The previous release answers healthy again |
| Rolled back, still unhealthy | The cause probably isn't the code (database, external service) |
| Rollback failed | The bad release is still live: act now |
| Nothing to roll back to | First release |

> [!warning] Off by default on purpose: **migrations are not undone**. Enable it for apps whose migrations are backwards-compatible, or pair it with [pre-deploy snapshots](https://cipi.sh/docs/safe-deploy).

Also in [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml) (`health:`), the REST API and the panel. To watch the server rather than the app, see [Server monitor](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor).


## Server monitor

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor

The server watches itself every 5 minutes and tells you when something actually breaks. No agent, no metrics database, no third-party service: a cron job, a few state files and your [notification channels](https://cipi.sh/docs/notifications).

```bash
$ cipi monitor                    # run every check now (exit 1 on warn/crit)
$ cipi monitor list               # checks, thresholds, state, last alert
$ cipi monitor set disk --warn=85 --crit=95
$ cipi monitor disable load
$ cipi monitor test               # sample alert to every channel
```

## Eight checks, on by default 

| Check | Watches | Alerts when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `disk` | Every local filesystem | ≥80% warn, ≥90% critical |
| `app_disk` | Apps with a [soft disk limit](https://cipi.sh/docs/limits#disk) | ≥90% of the limit, then over it |
| `ssl` | Let's Encrypt certificates | ≤14 days to expiry, or expired |
| `services` | Nginx, databases, PHP-FPM, Valkey, Supervisor, Fail2ban… | Any unit not active |
| `workers` | Queue workers and Horizon | A process not running |
| `http_5xx` | New lines in each app's access log | ≥20 errors **and** ≥5% of requests |
| `fs` | `/etc/cipi`, `/var/log/cipi` | No longer writable (read-only remount) |
| `load` | 1-minute load | Above 4× the cores for 2 runs in a row |

Tune any threshold: `--ssl --days=21`, `http_5xx --count=50 --ratio=10`, `load --factor=6 --runs=3`, `app_disk --minutes=30`.

## Alerts without noise 

| State change | Message |
| --- | --- |
| ok → warn/critical | One alert |
| warn ↔ critical | One escalation |
| Still failing | A reminder every 4 hours (`set reminder --minutes=N`, min 15) |
| failing → ok | One recovery, with how long it lasted |

The 5xx check reads only what was written since the last run and starts with a baseline, so it never alerts on old errors. A check that can't run reports critical instead of crashing. Each check has its own trigger and can be muted (`cipi notifications disable monitor_load`).

## In the web panel 

The fleet dashboard and each server's health. The [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) is optional; everything here also works from the CLI.


## Disk usage

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/disk

The [monitor](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor) tells you the disk is filling up; `cipi disk` tells you **who** is filling it.

```bash
$ cipi disk              # filesystems, then every app, largest first
$ cipi disk db           # every database of every engine
$ cipi disk --json       # for scripts (also: cipi disk db --json)
```

```text
 Server disk
 MOUNT  SIZE       USED      FREE      USE
 /      100.00 GB  40.00 GB  60.00 GB  40%

 Apps (3) — % of the 100.00 GB on /
 APP    FILES    DATABASE  TOTAL    DISK  LIMIT
 shop   2.00 GB  1.00 GB   3.00 GB  3.0%  10 GB (30%)
 blog   0.50 GB  120.4 MB  0.62 GB  0.6%  —
 All apps                  3.62 GB  3.6%
 Everything else          36.38 GB 36.4%
```

| Column | Measures |
| --- | --- |
| FILES | The app's home: releases, storage, logs |
| DATABASE | Its database (and the one `.env` points to, if different) |
| TOTAL / DISK | Files + database, and its share of the disk |
| LIMIT | The [soft disk limit](https://cipi.sh/docs/limits#disk) and how much is used |
| Everything else | System, packages, local backups, databases that belong to no app |

`cipi disk db` lists MariaDB and PostgreSQL databases, Valkey key counts and memory, and Meilisearch indexes with document counts, each engine with its total on disk. From your laptop: `cipi-cli disk`; in the panel: Server → Disk.

> [!note] Limits are soft by design: they alert, they never take a site down. Hard quotas couldn't cover the database and would break the app at the worst moment.


## Notifications

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/notifications

Cipi tells you when something happens that you should know about: failed deploys and backups, health and monitor alerts, security events (SSH logins, sudo, key changes), patches applied. One command manages where messages go; every enabled trigger reaches every enabled channel.

```bash
$ cipi notification                     # channels and active triggers (no secrets shown)
$ cipi notification add slack ops --url=https://hooks.slack.com/services/…
$ cipi notification test all
$ cipi notification triggers            # which events notify
$ cipi notification triggers disable monitor_load
```

## Channels 

| Type | Options | Delivers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `smtp` | `--host --port --user --password --from --to --tls` | Email via any SMTP server |
| `resend` | `--api-key --from --to` | Email via the Resend API |
| `ses` | `--region --access-key --secret-key --from --to` | Email via Amazon SES (signed by Cipi, no AWS CLI) |
| `slack`, `mattermost`, `googlechat` | `--url` (incoming webhook) | A chat message |
| `discord` | `--url` | A chat message (2 000-char cap) |
| `telegram` | `--token --chat-id` | Plain-text bot message |
| `ntfy` | `--url [--priority]` | Push notification; urgent events raised to high |
| `pushover` | `--token --user` | Push notification |
| `webhook` | `--url [--secret]` | JSON, optionally signed (`X-Cipi-Signature`) |

```bash
$ cipi notification add smtp --host=smtp.example.com --port=587 --user=… --password=… \
    --from=alerts@example.com --to=ops@example.com --tls=on
$ cipi notification add telegram oncall --token= --chat-id=
$ cipi notification add webhook pager --url=https://example.com/hooks/cipi --secret=…
$ cipi notification disable ops | enable ops | remove ops
```

Secrets omitted from the command line are asked for without echo, stored encrypted, and never printed back. Delivery is **best-effort with a 5-second timeout**: a dead webhook can never stall a deploy or a cron job.

```php
// verify a signed webhook (body: server, trigger, subject, body, ts)
$expected = 'sha256='.hash_hmac('sha256', file_get_contents('php://input'), $secret);
if (! hash_equals($expected, $_SERVER['HTTP_X_CIPI_SIGNATURE'] ?? '')) { http_response_code(401); exit; }
```

## Triggers 

All on by default; every event is also written to `/var/log/cipi/events.log` (kept a year) whatever you mute.

| Category | Triggers |
| --- | --- |
| Deploy | `deploy_success`, `deploy_fail`, `deploy_rollback`, `deploy_snapshot_fail`, `deploy_health_fail` |
| Health & monitor | `health_fail`, `monitor_disk`, `monitor_app_disk`, `monitor_ssl`, `monitor_services`, `monitor_workers`, `monitor_http_5xx`, `monitor_fs`, `monitor_load`, `monitor_ok` |
| Backups & cron | `backup_fail`, `backup_stale`, `cron_fail` |
| Security | `ssh_login`, `sudo`, `su`, `ssh_key_add`, `ssh_key_remove`, `ssh_key_rename`, `credentials_show`, `zt_*` |
| Apps & domains | `app_create`, `app_edit`, `app_delete`, `app_suspend`, `alias_*`, `www_*`, `redirect_change`, `proxy_change`, `basicauth_*` |
| Updates | `self_update`, `php_upgrade`, `nginx_upgrade`, `mariadb_upgrade`, `pgsql_upgrade`, `valkey_upgrade`, `node_upgrade`, `composer_upgrade`, `frankenphp_upgrade`, `pending_report` |
| Config | `ini_set`, `app_jit`, `yml_apply`, `yml_fail`, `yml_post_fail`, `node_default` |
| Other | SSL, PHP, database, workers, services, search, packages, sync, API and password-reset events |

`cipi notification triggers` prints the live list with on/off state; `enable-all`, `disable-all` and `reset` work as expected.

## Security alerts 

| Event | Includes |
| --- | --- |
| SSH login as root or a sudoer | Source IP, key fingerprint and comment |
| `sudo` / `su` | Who, target user, TTY, key, IP |
| SSH key added, removed, renamed | Fingerprint, comment, remaining keys |

They run in the background through PAM, so they never slow a login. Wrap your own cron jobs with `cipi-cron-notify` to be alerted when they exit non-zero.


## Log retention

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/log-retention

Logs rotate and expire automatically, with retention periods chosen for GDPR's data-minimisation principle. No manual cleanup, no disk filling up with years of access logs.

| Category | Logs | Kept |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Application | Laravel, PHP-FPM, workers, deploys, system | 12 months |
| Security | Fail2ban, firewall, authentication, Cipi events | 12 months |
| HTTP | Nginx access and error logs (contain IP addresses) | 90 days |

Logs are rotated daily and compressed from the second day. Laravel apps write a single `storage/logs/laravel.log` (`LOG_CHANNEL=single`) that follows the same policy. An app that sets `LOG_CHANNEL=daily` on purpose is pruned by Laravel itself (`LOG_DAILY_DAYS`).

> [!tip] Access logs hold IP addresses, which are personal data. 90 days is enough for debugging and incident analysis while keeping exposure low; application and security logs stay a year for audit trails.


## Security model

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/security-model

Security on Cipi is the default, not an add-on: apps are isolated from each other, the server is hardened at install, secrets are encrypted, and every privileged action leaves a trace. This page is the map; each layer links to its details.

```stack
Network | UFW 22/80/443, Fail2ban, CrowdSec, Zero Trust
Access | key-only admin, no root login, alerts
Isolation | user, PHP pool, database, Valkey per app
Secrets | AES-256 Vault, encrypted backups & sync
Patching | nightly PHP & stack patches, CVE reports
Audit | deploy ledger, event log, compliance
```

## Layers 

| Layer | What Cipi does | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Network** | UFW allows only 22, 80, 443. Fail2ban bans after 3 attempts, doubling up to 7 days; repeat offenders get a 7-day block. Unknown hostnames get an empty reply | [Firewall & bans](https://cipi.sh/docs/firewall), [Nginx](https://cipi.sh/docs/nginx#default-server) |
| **SSH** | Root login off; the `cipi` admin user is key-only; app users have their own password logins, which you can switch off | [SSH keys](https://cipi.sh/docs/ssh-keys) |
| **Privilege** | App users can't `su`; the web user's sudo is limited to an explicit list of `cipi` sub-commands; the API checks every command against a whitelist | [Panel architecture](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui-architecture) |
| **App isolation** | One Linux user per app (home `750`), its own PHP-FPM pool, `open_basedir` to its home, its own database user and Valkey instance | [How Cipi works](https://cipi.sh/docs/how-cipi-works#what-every-app-gets) |
| **Git** | A separate read-only deploy key per app; signed webhooks; deploys run as the app user | [Git](https://cipi.sh/docs/git), [Auto-deploy](https://cipi.sh/docs/auto-deploy) |
| **Secrets** | Configs, tokens and passwords encrypted at rest (AES-256); backups and sync archives encrypted before they leave | [Vault](https://cipi.sh/docs/vault), [Backups](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups#encryption) |
| **Patching** | Ubuntu security updates daily; PHP nightly with a patch-level report; Nginx, databases, Valkey, Node and FrankenPHP nightly, one at a time | [Stack upgrades](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades), [PHP](https://cipi.sh/docs/php#security) |
| **Hardening** | PHP pools lock down settings used by recent CVEs; Nginx never enables HTTP/2; TLS 1.2/1.3 with modern ciphers | [PHP](https://cipi.sh/docs/php#hardening), [Nginx](https://cipi.sh/docs/nginx) |
| **Detection** | Alerts on SSH logins, sudo/su, key changes; nightly malware scan; 5xx and service monitor | [Notifications](https://cipi.sh/docs/notifications#security), [Malware scan](https://cipi.sh/docs/malware-scan) |
| **Audit** | Hash-chained deploy ledger, one-year event log, ISO 27001 / SOC 2 evidence report | [Deploy audit](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit), [Compliance](https://cipi.sh/docs/compliance) |
| **Privacy** | No telemetry; logs with IP addresses kept 90 days | [Log retention](https://cipi.sh/docs/log-retention) |

## No web surface by default 

A fresh Cipi server has **no admin panel**: management happens over SSH. The [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui-overview) is opt-in, runs as an isolated app on its own domain with two-factor login, and talks to servers only through the API's whitelisted commands.

## What isolation protects 

If one app is compromised (a vulnerable plugin, a leaked `.env`), the attacker gets **that app's** user:

| They can't | Because |
| --- | --- |
| Read other apps' files | Homes are `750`, `open_basedir` confines PHP |
| Read other apps' data | Each database and Valkey instance has its own credentials |
| Become root or `cipi` | `su` is restricted to the sudo group; no sudo for app users |
| Read Cipi's secrets | Encrypted, readable by root only |
| Change the web server | Vhosts and pools are root-owned |
| Reuse the deploy key elsewhere | One key per repository, read-only |

> [!tip] Reboots after kernel updates are never automatic unless you enable [cipi reboot auto](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades#reboot); `cipi pending` tells you when one is due.


## Firewall & bans

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/firewall

UFW allows only SSH, HTTP and HTTPS; everything else is closed. Fail2ban bans addresses that keep failing SSH logins, longer each time.

```bash
$ cipi firewall list
$ cipi firewall allow 3306 --from=10.0.0.5        # one address
$ cipi firewall allow 3306 --from=10.0.0.0/24     # a private subnet
$ cipi firewall deny 8080
$ cipi firewall attempts [5|default]              # failed logins before a ban
```

| Protection | Default |
| --- | --- |
| Open ports | 22, 80, 443 |
| Failed SSH logins before a ban | 3 (counted over 1 hour) |
| Ban | 24 hours, doubling on each repeat, up to 7 days |
| Repeat offenders (`recidive`) | 3 bans in 24 h → 7 days |

The threshold is written to a drop-in that updates never reset, validated with `fail2ban-client -t` before reload (a rejected value changes nothing). Need a database port? Open it **to specific addresses only**, or better, connect over SSH with the `mariadb+ssh://` URL.

> [!tip] Behind Cloudflare, [cipi zt](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust) can close 80/443 to everyone but Cloudflare, and close 22 entirely.

## Bans 

```bash
$ cipi ban list                   # banned IPs, by jail (Fail2ban and CrowdSec)
$ cipi ban unban 203.0.113.42     # from every jail at once
```

Locked out a colleague or a CI runner by mistake? Unban from another session or the provider's console. For CI, use a dedicated key (key logins don't fail).


## SSH keys

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/ssh-keys

The `cipi` user is the admin entry point: **key-only**, no passwords, no root login. Manage its keys from the CLI, with guards against locking yourself out.

```bash
$ cipi ssh list                         # keys, fingerprints, current-session marker
$ cipi ssh add "ssh-ed25519 AAAA… john@laptop"
$ cipi ssh rename 2 "john-macbook"
$ cipi ssh remove 2
```

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Format validation, duplicate check | No broken or repeated keys |
| Current-session protection | You can't remove the key you're logged in with |
| Last-key protection | You can't remove the last key |
| Alerts | Every add, remove, rename notified with fingerprint and remaining count |

Also via REST (`GET|POST /api/ssh/keys`) and the panel.

## App users' SSH and SFTP 

Each app user can log in with its own password and keys; the server's admin keys always work for every app (`ssh shop@server` with your usual key). Decide per app, or for all of them, whether more is allowed from outside:

```bash
$ cipi ssh apps                    # every app: enabled or disabled
$ cipi ssh apps disable shop       # from outside: admin keys only
$ cipi ssh apps enable shop        # also its password and its own keys
$ cipi ssh apps disable --all      # every app, and new apps from now on
```

| State | From another machine | From the server (deploys) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enabled | Admin keys, app password, app's own keys | Unchanged |
| Disabled | Admin keys only | Unchanged |

New servers create apps **disabled** (safer for agencies handing out SFTP rarely). Changes are validated with `sshd -t` on a copy and applied with a reload, so a bad config never replaces the live one. Removing a key with `cipi ssh remove` revokes it for every app at once.


## Vault & encryption

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/vault

Every configuration file holding a secret (database passwords, API tokens, Git tokens, SMTP credentials, backup settings) is **encrypted at rest with AES-256**. A copy of `/etc/cipi` alone is useless without the key.

| Piece | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Master key | Generated at install, `/etc/cipi/.vault_key`, root-only (`400`) |
| Encrypted files | `server.json`, `apps.json`, `databases.json`, `backup.json`, `smtp.json`, `api.json`, alert channels, Git tokens |
| Cipher | `openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -salt -pbkdf2` |
| Public projection | `apps-public.json` holds only non-secret fields (domains, PHP, branch) for the panel API, so the key stays root-only |

```flow
Export (sync) | decrypt with this server's key
Archive | encrypted with your passphrase
Import | decrypt with the passphrase
Store | re-encrypted with the new server's key
```

Backups use their own key (`cipi backup key show`); sync archives use your passphrase. Keys never travel inside the data they protect.

> [!warning] Lose the vault key and the encrypted configs can't be read. Back it up with your server credentials (`cipi credentials export` lists the backup key; copy `.vault_key` to your password manager).


## CrowdSec

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/crowdsec

CrowdSec reads your Nginx logs, recognises attack patterns (scanners, credential stuffing, exploit probes), shares and receives a community blocklist, and a firewall bouncer drops the offending IPs. It complements Fail2ban; it is not a WAF. Off until you enable it.

```bash
$ cipi crowdsec enable                 # engine + firewall bouncer
$ cipi crowdsec status                 # engine, bouncer, rescue listener, decisions
$ cipi crowdsec allow 203.0.113.42     # never ban this address
$ cipi crowdsec disable                # flush rules first, then remove
```

## Safe by construction 

| Risk | Guard |
| --- | --- |
| Banning yourself | Your current SSH session is allowlisted before banning starts |
| Banning your CDN | Refused behind a proxy without real-IP config ([cipi zt enable](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust) writes it) |
| Banning your Git provider | GitHub and Bitbucket webhook ranges allowlisted (refreshed, fail-open); GitLab ranges included |
| Breaking renewals | Let's Encrypt validation, localhost and private ranges allowlisted |
| Too little RAM | Refused below 512 MB available |
| Orphan DROP rules after removal | `disable` flushes chains before purging packages |

It reads `/home/*/logs/nginx-*.log`, where every app's traffic is actually logged.

## Break-glass rescue 

Banned from your own server? `enable` starts a small TLS listener on a high port. One request with a one-shot token allowlists **your connecting IP** (never a header), lifts its bans in CrowdSec and Fail2ban, mails you a new token, and the old one dies.

```bash
$ cipi crowdsec rescue token     # print the curl command (keep it off the server)
$ cipi crowdsec rescue rotate    # new token, mailed to you
```

It grants nothing but the ability to connect again. The port is kept open ahead of CrowdSec's own rules; wrong tokens are throttled. `cipi ban list` and `cipi ban unban` cover CrowdSec too.


## Cloudflare Zero Trust

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust

Put your server behind Cloudflare: visitors reach apps through a Cloudflare Tunnel (with CDN and WAF), staging sites, the panel and SSH sit behind Cloudflare Access, and finally the origin closes its ports. Every step that could lock you out is a separate, explicit command. Off until you enable it.

```flow
Token | Tunnel, Access, DNS
Enable | tunnel + real IP; ports still open
Route | hostnames, Access, SSH
Test | from your laptop
Lock | 80/443 and 22 closed
```

```bash
$ cipi zt token set --token=CF_API_TOKEN --account=ACCOUNT_ID
$ cipi zt enable
$ cipi zt hostname add myapp           # public, through CDN/WAF
$ cipi zt access enable staging        # login required (Cloudflare Access)
$ cipi zt access enable --gui
$ cipi zt ssh enable --hostname=ssh.example.com
$ cipi zt lock http --yes              # 80/443 closed or Cloudflare-only
$ cipi zt lock ssh --yes               # port 22 closed
$ cipi zt status
```

Token permissions: Account · Cloudflare Tunnel: Edit, Account · Access: Apps and Policies: Edit, Zone · DNS: Edit (plus Zone · SSL and Certificates for Origin CA). It is stored root-only, separate from the DNS token used for certificates.

## What each step does 

| Command | Effect | Reversible with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enable` | Installs `cloudflared`, a locally-managed tunnel, Nginx real-IP from Cloudflare's ranges (refreshed daily); Fail2ban/CrowdSec learn the ranges. **No port is closed** | `disable` |
| `hostname add ` | DNS CNAME to the tunnel, ingress to Nginx | `hostname remove` |
| `access enable ` | Cloudflare Access login in front; `/cipi/webhook` bypassed so pushes still deploy | `access disable` |
| `ssh enable` | SSH through the tunnel + Access; prints your `~/.ssh/config` | `ssh disable` |
| `lock http` | 80/443 closed when everything is on the tunnel, else allowed from Cloudflare only | `unlock http` |
| `lock ssh` | Port 22 closed (only if the tunnel already carries SSH) | `ssh unlock` |

```text
# ~/.ssh/config on your laptop
Host ssh.example.com
  ProxyCommand cloudflared access ssh --hostname %h
  User cipi
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
```

> [!warning] Lock SSH only after `ssh ssh.example.com` works through the tunnel from your machine, and keep your provider's web console at hand. Deploys are unaffected (they use `localhost`).

## Certificates 

`lock http` refuses while an app still renews over HTTP (Let's Encrypt can't reach a closed origin). Move apps first to `cipi ssl install  --dns=cloudflare`, or use a 15-year Cloudflare Origin CA certificate:

```bash
$ cipi zt origin-cert myapp
```

Apps on the tunnel skip Cipi's HTTP→HTTPS redirect automatically (the tunnel talks HTTP to the origin and Cloudflare handles HTTPS). `cipi zt disable` reopens 22/80/443 and removes everything Cipi created in your Cloudflare account; Let's Encrypt certificates are left alone.


## Malware scan

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/malware-scan

Answers one question every night: **did anything change in this app that no deploy put there?** Integrity first, then ClamAV on upload folders. Off until you enable it.

```bash
$ cipi scan enable            # nightly at 04:40
$ cipi scan [myapp]           # now
$ cipi scan status | report
$ cipi scan manifest myapp    # re-baseline after a legitimate manual change
$ cipi scan disable
```

```flow
Every deploy | sha256 manifest of the release
Nightly | compare current/ to the manifest
Uploads | ClamAV + PHP webshell signatures
Report | changed or extra files, by email
```

| Design choice | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Manifests in `/var/lib/cipi/manifests`, root-only | A webshell in the app's home can't rewrite them |
| Antivirus only on upload folders | The manifest already covers everything a deploy put there; less noise, less RAM |
| Every re-baseline logged in `events.log` | A manifest rewrite without a deploy is the thing to look for |
| `scan_incomplete` is never called "clean" | A check that didn't finish told you nothing |
| Filenames compared exactly (spaces, backslashes) | Tricks like `sh\ell.php` can't hide |
| Refused below 2 GB free RAM / 3 GB on `/var` | ClamAV loads all signatures; an OOM kill could take the database down |

Alerts: `scan_integrity` (changed or extra files, plus PHP isolation drift) and `scan_incomplete`.

> [!note] It detects change between deploys; it doesn't prevent it. Isolation (per-app users, `open_basedir`) remains the first line of defence; this verifies it still holds.


## Compliance evidence

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/compliance

Under an ISO 27001 or SOC 2 audit, you need **evidence** that your hosting meets the controls. `cipi compliance` collects it from the server, read-only, in a form an auditor accepts.

```bash
$ cipi compliance                     # 17 controls: pass / warn / fail / info
$ cipi compliance tls --days=30       # one control
$ cipi compliance --json              # exit 1 on any fail: gate CI or cron
$ cipi compliance report [--days=365] # evidence bundle
$ cipi compliance controls            # mapping to ISO 27001:2022 Annex A and SOC 2
```

## Controls 

| Control | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| `ssh`, `ssh_keys`, `accounts` | Effective sshd config; key types and sizes; UID 0, empty passwords, sudoers |
| `firewall`, `intrusion`, `kernel` | UFW default deny; Fail2ban/CrowdSec; network sysctls |
| `patching`, `time` | Security updates, reboots pending; NTP |
| `tls` | Protocols, HSTS, certificate expiry and key type |
| `api_tokens`, `gui_2fa` | Token expiry, scope, IP allowlists; two-factor on panel accounts |
| `secrets` | Encrypted, root-only configuration |
| `deploys` | [Deploy audit](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit) chain intact, hooks present, no unaudited releases |
| `backups` | Freshness, off-site copy, encryption |
| `logging`, `monitoring` | Forwarding, history, auditd; monitor and alert delivery |
| `malware` | [Malware scan](https://cipi.sh/docs/malware-scan) enabled |

## The evidence bundle 

```tree
/var/log/cipi/compliance/-/
├── report.md          # for the auditor
├── report.json        # for tooling
├── evidence//…   # raw output behind each finding
└── SHA256SUMS         # + a .tar.gz and its checksum
```

Root-only. Record the printed archive checksum **outside the server** to prove later that the bundle is unaltered. No secrets are included: token and password hashes, 2FA secrets and backup credentials are never selected; SSH keys appear as fingerprints.

> [!note] The report is candid about limits (for example, encryption without a MAC, restore tests not recorded) so the auditor hears it from you first. Cipi's deliberate choices, like patching Nginx and databases on its own schedule, appear as notes, not failures.


## Install the agent

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-install

**Cipi Agent** (`cipi/agent`) is a Laravel package that connects your app to the server it runs on. Install it once and the app gains push-to-deploy, a health endpoint, an MCP server for AI assistants, `cipi.yml` tooling and a GDPR-friendly database anonymizer.

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent
$ git commit -am "Add Cipi Agent" && git push
$ php artisan cipi:status        # after the next deploy
```

On a Cipi server, `cipi app create` already wrote the `.env` variables the agent needs; the service provider auto-discovers. Health, MCP, `cipi.yml` validation and the anonymizer also work on any Laravel host.

## What you get 

| Feature | Endpoint / command | Read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Push-to-deploy | `POST /cipi/webhook` | [Webhook & health](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-webhook) |
| Health check | `GET /cipi/health` (Bearer token) | [Webhook & health](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-webhook#agent-health) |
| MCP server | `/cipi/mcp` | [MCP server](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp) |
| `cipi.yml` tooling | `php artisan cipi:yml` | [cipi.yml tooling](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-yml) |
| Anonymized dumps | `php artisan cipi:anonymize`, `/cipi/db` | [Database anonymizer](https://cipi.sh/docs/anonymizer) |
| Panel tools | MCP `panel_*` via `cipi/sdk` | [MCP server](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp#agent-mcp-panel) |

| Requirement | |
| --- | --- |
| PHP | 8.3+ |
| Laravel | 12 or 13 |
| Anonymizer | MySQL/MariaDB or PostgreSQL, with `mysqldump`/`pg_dump` on the server |
| Optional | `cipi/sdk` for panel tools; `ext-zlib` for gzip dumps |

## Artisan commands 

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi:status` | Configuration, environment, live release and commit, features, `cipi.yml` validity, DB connectivity |
| `cipi:mcp [--json]` | MCP endpoint, tools and ready-to-paste setup for Cursor, VS Code, Claude Code, Claude Desktop |
| `cipi:generate-token mcp\|health\|anonymize` | Create a secure token in `.env` |
| `cipi:service mcp\|health\|anonymize --enable\|--disable` | Toggle a feature |
| `cipi:deploy-key` | Print the app's deploy key |
| `cipi:yml validate\|show\|generate\|example\|schema` | [cipi.yml tooling](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-yml) |
| `cipi:init-anonymize [--scan]`, `cipi:anonymize-audit`, `cipi:anonymize` | [Anonymizer](https://cipi.sh/docs/anonymizer) |

```bash
$ php artisan vendor:publish --tag=cipi-agent-config    # only for custom defaults
```

> [!note] The agent runs **inside one app** (`/cipi/*` on its domain). The [REST API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) runs on its own domain and manages the **whole server**. Comparison: [Agent vs API](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp#agent-vs-api).


## Webhook & health check

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-webhook

## Push-to-deploy webhook 

`POST /cipi/webhook` verifies the push, checks the branch and drops a trigger file; within a minute the server deploys as the app user. The HTTP answer is instant, and the deploy never runs inside a web request. Full flow: [Auto-deploy on push](https://cipi.sh/docs/auto-deploy).

| Provider | Authentication | Event |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub | `X-Hub-Signature-256` (HMAC-SHA256, secret = `CIPI_WEBHOOK_TOKEN`) | `push` (`ping` answers `pong`) |
| GitLab | `X-Gitlab-Token` | Push Hook |
| Bitbucket Cloud | `X-Hub-Signature` (HMAC) | `repo:push` |
| Gitea / Forgejo | `X-Gitea-Signature` (HMAC) | `push` |
| Azure DevOps | `X-Gitlab-Token` (set by Cipi's service hook) | `git.push` |

Only pushes to `CIPI_DEPLOY_BRANCH` deploy (others answer `skipped`); other events answer `202 ignored`. Get URL and token with `cipi deploy myapp --webhook`.

Each trigger records what the push claimed (provider, pusher, commit, delivery ID, IP) for the [deploy audit](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit):

```json
{"source":"github","actor":"octocat","ip":"140.82.115.3","ref":"main@abcdef123456","request_id":"8d2f…"}
```

## Health endpoint 

`GET /cipi/health` returns the state of app, database, cache, queue, storage and the deploy. Plug it into UptimeRobot, Better Stack, Grafana or a simple cron.

```bash
$ php artisan cipi:generate-token health
$ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CIPI_HEALTH_TOKEN" https://myapp.com/cipi/health
```

```json
{
  "status": "healthy",
  "environment": "production",
  "checks": {
    "app": { "ok": true, "debug": false, "maintenance": false },
    "database": { "ok": true, "driver": "mysql" },
    "cache": { "ok": true, "driver": "database" },
    "queue": { "ok": true, "pending_jobs": 0, "failed_jobs": 0 },
    "storage": { "ok": true, "disk_free_gb": 31.2, "disk_used_percent": 41 },
    "deploy": { "ok": true, "short_commit": "0123456", "in_progress": false,
                "last_deploy": { "status": "ok", "trigger": "webhook", "duration_seconds": 42 } }
  }
}
```

| Field | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `status` | `degraded` (HTTP 503) if database, cache, queue or storage fails |
| `checks.queue.failed_jobs` / `pending_jobs` | Alert on stuck jobs or backlog |
| `checks.storage.disk_used_percent` | Disk pressure |
| `checks.deploy` | Live release and commit; a failed last deploy is informational (the previous release is still serving) |

Token order: `CIPI_HEALTH_TOKEN`, then `CIPI_WEBHOOK_TOKEN`. Disable with `php artisan cipi:service health --disable`.


## MCP server

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp

Talk to production from Claude, Cursor or VS Code: *"is the app healthy, what failed last night, deploy main"*. The agent's MCP server exposes **one app** to your assistant over HTTPS, with a token, guardrails and secret redaction. No SSH access needed.

```bash
$ php artisan cipi:service mcp --enable
$ php artisan cipi:generate-token mcp
$ php artisan cipi:mcp             # endpoint + ready-to-paste client config
```

Step-by-step with real prompts: [Manage Laravel in production with Claude and the Cipi MCP](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents).

## Two MCP servers 

| | Agent MCP | Server MCP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Endpoint | `https://myapp.com/cipi/mcp` | `https://api.example.com/mcp` |
| Scope | One app: logs, DB, Artisan, deploy, `cipi.yml` | The whole server: create apps, SSL, databases, backups |
| Installed with | `composer require cipi/agent` | `cipi api api.example.com` |
| Use for | Debugging and deploying an app | Operating the server |

## Tools 

| Tool | Mode | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `health` | read | App, database, cache, queue, storage, deploy state |
| `app_info` | read | Versions, drivers, features, environment, live commit; never secrets |
| `deploy_status` | read | Live release, rollback candidates, running/queued, last outcome, log tail |
| `logs` | read | `laravel`, `nginx`, `php`, `worker`, `horizon`, `reverb`, `deploy`; level and keyword filters |
| `db_schema` | read | Tables, columns, indexes, foreign keys; flags likely personal data |
| `env_check` | read | Which keys are set or missing vs `.env.example` and `cipi.yml`; names only |
| `cipi_yml` | read | Validate a draft, show, generate or example |
| `db_query` | configurable | Reads capped at 100 rows; writes unless `CIPI_MCP_DB_WRITE=false` |
| `artisan` | may change data | Runs commands non-interactively; dangerous ones blocked |
| `deploy` | action | Queues a zero-downtime deploy; records who asked in the audit ledger |
| `anonymizer` | action | Audit, scan, or start an anonymized dump |
| `panel_*` | via `cipi/sdk` | Rollback, audit ledger, DB backup, job status, server status |

Resources: `cipi://cipi.yml`, its schema and example, `cipi://anonymization.json` and its schema.

## Guardrails 

| Guard | Blocks |
| --- | --- |
| Artisan blocklist | `tinker`, `serve`, `queue:work`, `horizon`, `octane:start`, `reverb:start`, `db:wipe`, `migrate:fresh`, `migrate:reset`… (extendable) |
| SQL guard | DDL (`DROP`, `ALTER`, `TRUNCATE`, `CREATE`), `GRANT`, file I/O, `SET GLOBAL`, `KILL`, multi-statements |
| Redaction | Env assignments, bearer tokens, DSNs, `APP_KEY`, provider keys masked in output |
