Free and polished, for PHP, Node, Python and static sites. A generic multi-stack panel with no Laravel release or worker management. Pick it if Python sites matter to you; pick Cipi for Laravel depth. [Cipi vs CloudPanel](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-cloudpanel).

## Managed PaaS 

You don't touch a server; you pay for resources and accept the platform's limits.

| Platform | Strength | Choose Cipi when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Laravel Cloud](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-laravel-cloud) | Autoscaling, scale-to-zero, managed databases and edge, from the Laravel team | You want a fixed bill, root and a portable stack |
| [Ploi Cloud](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-ploi-cloud) | EU PaaS for Laravel, PHP and Node, memory-based pricing | You'd rather own the VPS and pay the provider only |
| [Render](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-render) | Multi-language, previews, private networking, compliance options | Your apps are Laravel/PHP and you want no usage invoice |
| [Sevalla](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-sevalla) | Apps, databases and storage under one managed bill | You want native Laravel on your own Ubuntu |
| [fortrabbit](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-fortrabbit) | PHP-specialised managed hosting with a long track record | You want root, Octane, Horizon and Reverb under your control |

## Self-hosted Docker PaaS 

[Coolify](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-coolify), [Dokku](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-dokku) and [Easypanel](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-easypanel) deploy containers on your server, free. Great when you host many stacks and already think in Docker. Cipi runs a **native** Nginx + PHP-FPM/Octane + MariaDB/PostgreSQL stack with no container layer: less overhead, simpler debugging, and Laravel's lifecycle (releases, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb) built in.

## Deploy tools 

[Kamal](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-kamal) ships containers over SSH to servers you've already prepared. It doesn't install the web server, PHP, databases, firewall, certificates, backups or workers. Cipi does all of that, and deploys. Choose Kamal if you have Docker infrastructure and need only the deploy step.

## Hosting panels 

[cPanel](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-cpanel), [Plesk](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-plesk) and [DirectAdmin](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-directadmin) are built for selling shared hosting: e-mail, FTP, DNS and many customer sites, under a licence. Right for hosting resellers, heavy for a team deploying its own apps.

HestiaCP (the maintained fork of the abandoned VestaCP) is a free, lighter alternative for e-mail, DNS and many websites, with no Laravel tooling. aaPanel is a free, plugin-based multi-stack panel popular in Asia-Pacific, GUI-centric, also without Laravel automation.

GridPane, xCloud and ServerAvatar focus on WordPress and WooCommerce: staging clones, multisite, WordPress caching. For WordPress fleets, evaluate them on their merits. Cipi runs WordPress as a custom app when it sits next to your Laravel apps.

20i is a hosting company (reseller, WordPress, VPS, domains, e-mail, 24×7 support). It covers a full hosting catalogue; Cipi replaces it only for "deploy my apps on a VPS I own". Cipi vs 20i.

## How to choose 

```flow
Own a VPS? | no → managed PaaS
Laravel or PHP apps? | many stacks → Docker PaaS
Want to pay per server? | yes → Forge or Ploi
Otherwise | Cipi
```


## Design decisions

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/design-decisions

## Why not local? 

Cipi is a **production server provisioner**: it turns a fresh Ubuntu VPS into an internet-facing host. It doesn't run on a laptop, in local Docker, or behind a home NAT, by design.

| A Cipi server needs | Because |
| --- | --- |
| A public IPv4 address, no NAT | Domains must resolve to it and Git providers must reach its webhooks |
| Full virtualization or bare metal (KVM, VMware, Hyper-V, Xen HVM) | Shared-kernel containers (OpenVZ, LXC) can't run the services and firewall Cipi manages; the installer detects them and stops |
| Ports 22, 80 and 443 reachable | SSH, Let's Encrypt validation and HTTPS |

> [!warning] Don't install Cipi inside Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Colima, WSL or a local VM expecting a working stack: certificates won't issue, domains won't resolve and webhooks can't arrive. A small VPS is enough for staging.

Every production provisioner has the same constraint. What Cipi doesn't ask for is the difference: no agent phoning home, no external control plane, no cloud account.

**Locally**, use [Laravel Herd](https://herd.laravel.com/), [Sail](https://laravel.com/docs/sail) or `php artisan serve`, then push to a Cipi server for staging and production.

## Why MariaDB by default? 

MariaDB (port `3306`) is the default because it fits most Laravel apps with zero friction. [PostgreSQL](#why-postgresql) is one command away and can run next to it.

| Reason | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Drop-in for Laravel | `mysql` driver, same `DB_*` keys, same migrations; works with TablePlus, DBeaver, Sequel Ace |
| Built for web concurrency | Strong optimizer and a native thread pool in the community edition, good with PHP-FPM connection churn |
| Tuned to your VPS | Cipi sizes `innodb_buffer_pool_size` from RAM (256 MB on 1 GB hosts up to 4 GB on 16 GB+) |
| Simple licensing | GPL community server, no enterprise feature gates, no Oracle dual-licensing to navigate |
| Native packaging | Installed from MariaDB.org or Ubuntu; Cipi adds users, backups and vault credentials on top |

## Why PostgreSQL as an option? 

```bash
$ cipi db install pgsql                       # port 5432, side by side with MariaDB
$ cipi app create shop --engine=pgsql
```

Choose PostgreSQL per app when the product needs more than tables:

| Need | PostgreSQL gives you |
| --- | --- |
| Rich data | JSONB, arrays, ranges, UUID, full-text search, CHECK and exclusion constraints |
| Indexing | B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, partial and expression indexes |
| Extensions | `pgcrypto`, `pg_trgm`, PostGIS, `pgvector` for embeddings and RAG |
| Concurrency | MVCC: readers don't block writers; long reports and busy writes coexist |
| Portability | The standard of managed databases, BI tools and data pipelines |

The same `cipi db` workflow covers both engines: create, list, backup, restore, password rotation.

## Why Valkey? 

| Reason | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Drop-in | Same protocol on `6379`, same `phpredis`, same `REDIS_*` keys; Laravel doesn't notice |
| Truly open source | BSD-licensed, stewarded by the Linux Foundation after Redis moved to source-available licences |
| Native on Ubuntu | `valkey-server` from the Universe repository, no third-party PPAs |
| Automatic migration | Servers moved from Redis to Valkey on `cipi self-update`, same password and data |

## Why Laravel first? 

Knowing the framework lets Cipi automate what generic panels leave to you: the release layout, `.env` handling, queue workers, the scheduler, Horizon, Reverb, Octane, health routes. Every assumption maps to a known structure, so there's no guesswork. Anything that isn't Laravel still runs as a [custom app](https://cipi.sh/docs/custom-apps) (WordPress, Symfony, static sites) or a [Node app](https://cipi.sh/docs/node-apps).

| Laravel brings | Cipi turns it into |
| --- | --- |
| Queues and Horizon | Supervisor workers, `cipi worker horizon enable` |
| Reverb | Supervisor process, Nginx `/app` proxy, `REVERB_*` keys: `cipi app reverb enable` |
| Octane | FrankenPHP apps side by side with FPM: `cipi app create --octane` |
| Scheduler | One cron per app, nothing to configure |
| Scout | Meilisearch on the server: `cipi search` |
| Secure defaults and a long support cycle | Apps you can leave in production for years |

Taylor Otwell's mantra is **"we must ship"**. Cipi exists for the same reason: to remove the server work between a developer and a live application.

## Why "ci-pi"? 

Cipi is the Italian reading of the letters C and P: Control Panel. A nod to the project's Italian roots, and to what it does under the hood: manage Nginx, PHP-FPM, databases, Supervisor, certificates and the firewall for you.

The mascot is a penguin, a reference to **Tux**, the Linux mascot drawn by Larry Ewing in 1996. Same species, different attitude: minimal, hand-sketched, happier in the terminal than in the spotlight.


## History

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/history

Cipi was created by [Andrea Pollastri](https://web.ap.it), a developer since 2005 working on Laravel, system administration and security, with experience at companies like Docebo and Musement. He built it out of a practical need: a fast, scriptable way to put Laravel apps on his own VPS without handing control to a SaaS panel. The private tool became an open-source project with over 1,000 GitHub stars and servers running it around the world.

Seven years, five major versions, one idea that never changed: **your server, your apps, no bill for the tool.**

v0.1June 2019The ideaA handful of shell scripts that set up Nginx, PHP, MariaDB and Supervisor on a fresh Ubuntu VPS. No UI, no package. Just bash.
v1–v22019–2020A Laravel control panelThe scripts were wrapped in a Laravel web panel hosted on the same server: create apps, deploy, configure Nginx from the browser. A year of iteration added SMTP, database backups, service management and dozens of fixes, and Cipi became a stable choice for small-team Laravel hosting.
v32021API, PHP 8, real-time UIRebuilt on Laravel 8 with a documented REST API, PHP 8, live CPU and RAM charts, a cron editor, Supervisor and GitHub management. The 3.1 series was the most polished release of the web-UI era, and many teams ran it for years. It also raised the question that shaped what followed: was a browser panel still the right interface, when deploys were moving to SSH, CI pipelines and automation?
v42026The rewrite: CLI-first, Laravel-firstThe web UI was dropped and Cipi became a CLI operated over SSH, with every part of the stack tuned for Laravel. MariaDB replaced MySQL, Deployer brought zero-downtime releases, each app got its own Linux user and deploy key, and GitHub and GitLab webhooks, S3 backups, encrypted server sync, a REST API and MCP servers for AI agents arrived. Late v4 added optional PostgreSQL and the return of a web panel, this time as an optional add-on.
v52026, todayA complete, free platform on your own serverv5 turned the CLI into a full replacement for paid server panels, without giving up what made it simple. One command installs a hardened server; apps are isolated cells with their own user, PHP pool, database and certificate; deploys are atomic, audited and rolled back in one step.

## Cipi today 

| Area | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| Apps | Laravel on PHP-FPM or Octane (FrankenPHP), Node apps (SPA, static, SSR), and custom PHP apps such as WordPress or Symfony |
| Deploy | Zero-downtime releases, Git push from six forges, preview environments, a hash-chained audit trail, health-checked rollbacks |
| `cipi.yml` | The app's server settings versioned in its repository: PHP, workers, schedule, domains, databases, backups, per environment |
| Runtime | Multiple PHP versions side by side, MariaDB and PostgreSQL, Valkey, Meilisearch, Horizon and Reverb |
| Operations | Backup profiles to S3 with verification, server monitor, health checks, disk usage, alerts by e-mail, Slack, Telegram and webhooks |
| Security | Per-app isolation, encrypted vault, firewall and CrowdSec, Cloudflare Zero Trust, malware scans, automatic PHP and Nginx security updates |
| Interfaces | The CLI, an optional web panel with roles and SSO, a REST API, cipi-cli, a PHP SDK, WHMCS and MCP servers for AI assistants |

Every version is listed in the [changelog](https://github.com/cipi-sh/cipi/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md). Announcements go out first on the [Telegram channel](https://t.me/cipicloud).


## Companion tools & community

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/community

## Companion tools 

Cipi deploys and runs your apps. Exception tracking, analytics or object storage are separate jobs, better done by separate tools. These projects cover the gaps around a Cipi server: same author, open source, all optional. Cipi depends on none of them.

### Around the server 

| Tool | What it does | With Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [**conn**](https://conn.web.ap.it/) | SSH connection manager: save connections under aliases, connect with `conn to ` | One alias for the `cipi` admin user and one per app user, instead of remembering hosts and ports |
| [**Johnny**](https://johnny.web.ap.it/) | S3-compatible object storage on your own VPS (Garage + Caddy), with a web panel, CLI and API | On a **separate** VPS, as the S3 destination for [`cipi backup`](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups) or a Laravel disk: off-site, still yours |

### Monitoring and analytics 

| Tool | What it does | With Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [**Boogle**](https://boogle.web.ap.it/) | Self-hosted exception tracker and uptime monitor for Laravel | [`cipi monitor`](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor) watches the server, Boogle the application from outside. Error payloads stay on your infrastructure |
| [**IndieStats**](https://indiestats.web.ap.it/) | Privacy-friendly web analytics on Laravel: no cookies, no consent banner | Deploy it with `cipi app create` on a subdomain and track every site without sending visitor data anywhere |

### Application security 

| Tool | What it does | With Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [**Checkpoint**](https://checkpoint.web.ap.it/) | Laravel security audit in one Artisan command: vulnerable dependencies, leaked secrets, injection risks | Cipi hardens the server, Checkpoint the code. Run it in CI before the deploy |
| [**Hackly**](https://hackly.web.ap.it/) | Authorized attack-surface and code scanning (Laravel/PHP SAST and SCA) with a Filament panel | A continuous vulnerability view across projects; runs on a Cipi server, pairs with [`cipi compliance`](https://cipi.sh/docs/compliance) |

### Building Laravel apps 

| Tool | What it does | With Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [**init**](https://init.web.ap.it/) | One command for a complete local Laravel + Filament stack on macOS, with Docker, SSL and a real subdomain | Start locally, push to Git, and let Cipi take over: [Git setup](https://cipi.sh/docs/git), [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml), zero-downtime deploys |
| [**Larapilot**](https://larapilot.web.ap.it/) | Spec-driven AI workflow for Laravel via Laravel Boost: from product idea to reviewed code | Larapilot shapes the code; the [agent's MCP server](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp) and the [Cipi API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) let the same AI see and operate the running app |
| [**Studio**](https://studio.web.ap.it/) | Self-hosted, browser-based hub for teams building Laravel: each person's Claude Code writes and ships code, admins decide per project who sees and approves what, with previews, Git repositories, connectors, passwords and backups | Runs on its own Ubuntu VPS. Studio is where the team writes and reviews code; Cipi is where it goes live |

# Guides


## Deploy Laravel on an Ubuntu VPS with zero downtime

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps

This guide takes a fresh VPS to a live Laravel app with HTTPS, a queue worker, the scheduler and deploys on every `git push`. It uses [Cipi](https://cipi.sh/), a free, open-source tool that installs and runs the whole stack on your own server.

```flow
Server | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04
Install | one command, ~10 min
App | isolated user, DB, PHP
Deploy | atomic release from Git
HTTPS | Let's Encrypt
```

**You need:** a VPS with a public IPv4 (1 GB RAM is enough to start, 2 GB is comfortable), a domain whose DNS you control, and your Laravel project in a Git repository (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps or any server that accepts SSH deploy keys).

## 1. Create the server

Pick any provider that gives you a full virtual machine with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 LTS: Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS, Vultr, Linode, OVHcloud, Scaleway. Provider-specific walkthroughs: [AWS EC2](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-ec2), [Lightsail](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-lightsail), [DigitalOcean](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-digitalocean), [Hetzner](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-hetzner).

Open ports **22, 80 and 443** in the provider's firewall if it has one. Then point your domain's `A` record at the server's IP; DNS can propagate while you install.

## 2. Install Cipi

SSH in as root (or a sudo user) and run the installer:

```bash
$ ssh root@203.0.113.10
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

It asks for your SSH public key, shows what it will do, and only then installs Nginx, PHP, MariaDB, Valkey, Supervisor, Node, Certbot, the firewall and fail2ban, and hardens SSH. Save the credentials it prints: they're shown once.

## 3. Log in as cipi

Root login is now disabled. Connect as `cipi` with your key; Cipi commands run with `sudo`, no password.

```bash
$ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10
$ sudo cipi status
```

## 4. Create the app

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.6
```

Or run `sudo cipi app create` alone and answer the wizard. Cipi creates a Linux user `shop`, a database and user `shop`, a PHP-FPM pool, an Nginx vhost, a queue worker, the scheduler cron and an `ed25519` deploy key.

| You get | Where |
| --- | --- |
| `.env` with every credential | `/home/shop/shared/.env` |
| Releases | `/home/shop/releases/`, live one linked at `current/` |
| Logs | `/home/shop/logs/` |
| One-time summary | DB password, deploy key, webhook URL and token |

## 5. Connect the repository

Add the deploy key from the summary as a **read-only deploy key** (GitHub: Settings → Deploy keys), and the webhook URL and token if you want push-to-deploy. If you gave Cipi a Git token, it already did both. Check access:

```bash
$ sudo cipi git check shop
```

## 6. Deploy

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop
```

Each deploy clones into a new release folder, runs `composer install`, links `.env` and `storage`, runs migrations, builds assets if you set a build command, then switches `current` with one atomic symlink and restarts workers. Visitors never see a half-deployed app.

## 7. Turn on HTTPS

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop
```

The certificate covers the domain and every alias and renews by itself. `APP_URL` becomes `https://`. Behind the Cloudflare proxy, use `--dns=cloudflare` and set SSL/TLS to Full (strict).

## 8. Deploy on every push

With the webhook in place, every push to `main` deploys. Prefer tests first? Turn the webhook off and deploy from [GitHub Actions](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow). Want the server settings (PHP, workers, backups) versioned in the repository? Add a [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml).

## What to do next

| Goal | Command or guide |
| --- | --- |
| Roll back | `sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback` |
| More queue workers or Horizon | [Horizon and queues](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues) |
| Nightly backups to S3 | [Back up to S3](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3) |
| Faster responses | [Laravel Octane with FrankenPHP](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-octane-frankenphp) |
| Alerts on Telegram or Slack | [Monitoring and alerts](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts) |
| A browser UI for the team | [Web panel and API](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-gui-and-api) |


## Install Cipi on AWS EC2

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-ec2

EC2 gives you a full virtual machine, which is exactly what Cipi needs. This walkthrough uses the AWS console; the same settings work from Terraform or the CLI.

```flow
Launch | Ubuntu 24.04 LTS
Security group | 22, 80, 443
Elastic IP | stable public address
Install | wget … | bash
DNS | A record → Elastic IP
```

## 1. Launch the instance

In **EC2 → Launch instance**:

| Setting | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| AMI | **Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS** (or 26.04 LTS), from Canonical |
| Instance type | 2 GB RAM or more to be comfortable |
| Key pair | Your existing key, or create one and download it |
| Storage | 30 GB gp3 or more (releases, logs and local backups live here) |
| Network | A public subnet, **Auto-assign public IP** on |

## 2. Open the ports

Create a security group with inbound rules:

| Port | Source | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 22 (SSH) | Your IP, or anywhere if you'll rely on Cipi's fail2ban and keys | Administration |
| 80 (HTTP) | Anywhere (IPv4 and IPv6) | Let's Encrypt validation, redirects |
| 443 (HTTPS) | Anywhere (IPv4 and IPv6) | Your apps |

Cipi also runs its own firewall (UFW) on the instance; the two layers don't conflict.

## 3. Attach an Elastic IP

**EC2 → Elastic IPs → Allocate**, then **Associate** it with the instance. The public IP of an instance changes on stop/start; your DNS shouldn't.

## 4. Install Cipi

EC2 logs you in as `ubuntu` (a sudo user), not root:

```bash
$ ssh -i ~/Downloads/my-key.pem ubuntu@203.0.113.10
$ sudo -i
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

When the installer asks for your SSH public key, paste the **public** half of the key you'll use from now on (`cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` on your laptop). After the install you log in as `cipi`:

```bash
$ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10
$ sudo cipi status
```

## 5. Point DNS and create the first app

Create an `A` record (Route 53 or your DNS provider) for your domain to the Elastic IP, then follow [Deploy Laravel on an Ubuntu VPS](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps) from step 4.

## AWS services that fit well

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Off-site backups | An S3 bucket as destination: `sudo cipi backup configure` ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3)) |
| Outgoing mail | Amazon SES SMTP credentials in the app's `.env` |
| Code on AWS | CodeCommit works with Cipi's automatic deploy keys |
| Snapshots of the whole disk | EBS snapshots, on top of Cipi's database and file backups |

> [!tip] Outbound port 25 is restricted on EC2 by default. Use SES or another provider on port 587 for app mail and for Cipi's [notifications](https://cipi.sh/docs/notifications).


## Install Cipi on Amazon Lightsail

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-lightsail

Lightsail is AWS with a fixed monthly price: a good fit for one to a handful of apps. Use the **OS-only** Ubuntu blueprint so Cipi can own the stack.

## 1. Create the instance

**Lightsail → Create instance**:

| Setting | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| Platform | Linux/Unix |
| Blueprint | **OS Only → Ubuntu 24.04 LTS** (not LAMP or a Bitnami app) |
| SSH key | Your own key, or the default one Lightsail generates |
| Plan | 2 GB RAM is comfortable; 1 GB works for a small app |

## 2. Static IP and firewall

- **Networking → Create static IP** and attach it to the instance.
- In the instance's **Networking** tab, IPv4 firewall: keep SSH (22) and HTTP (80), **add HTTPS (443)**. Do the same for IPv6 if you use it.

## 3. Install Cipi

```bash
$ ssh ubuntu@203.0.113.10
$ sudo -i
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

Paste your own public key when asked. From then on: `ssh cipi@203.0.113.10` and `sudo cipi …`.

## 4. DNS and first app

Point an `A` record at the static IP (Lightsail DNS zones work), then create and deploy the app as in [the main guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps).

## Growing out of it

| When | Do |
| --- | --- |
| You need more RAM | Snapshot the instance and create a bigger one from it, or move apps with [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) |
| You need VPC, autoscaling groups, RDS in private subnets | Move to [EC2](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-ec2) |

> [!note] Lightsail's own snapshots copy the whole disk. Keep Cipi's [S3 backups](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3) too: they're per app, encrypted and restorable on any server.


## Install Cipi on a DigitalOcean Droplet

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-digitalocean

A Droplet is a full KVM virtual machine: exactly what Cipi needs.

## 1. Create the Droplet

**Create → Droplets**:

| Setting | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| Image | **Ubuntu 24.04 (LTS) x64** |
| Size | Basic, 2 GB RAM is comfortable for a few apps |
| Authentication | **SSH key** (add yours) |
| Extras | Monitoring agent optional; Cipi has its own [monitor](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor) |

## 2. Firewall and IP

- **Networking → Firewalls**: inbound TCP 22, 80, 443 from all IPv4 and IPv6; attach to the Droplet. Optional: Cipi's own firewall already protects the host.
- **Networking → Reserved IPs**: assign one if you may rebuild or resize the Droplet.

## 3. Install

```bash
$ ssh root@203.0.113.10
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

The installer disables root login and creates the `cipi` user with your key. Then:

```bash
$ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10
$ sudo cipi status
```

## 4. DNS and first app

Add an `A` record (DigitalOcean DNS or your registrar) to the Droplet's IP and continue with [Deploy Laravel on an Ubuntu VPS](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps).

## DigitalOcean extras that fit

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Off-site backups | **Spaces** is S3-compatible: use it as a `cipi backup` destination |
| Managed database | Point `DB_*` at a Managed MySQL/PostgreSQL cluster if you prefer |
| Behind a load balancer | Terminate TLS on the balancer or pass through to Cipi's certificates |


## Install Cipi on Hetzner Cloud

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-hetzner

Hetzner Cloud is a popular choice for Laravel in Europe: KVM servers at low prices, with data centres in Germany and Finland as well as the US and Singapore. Data stays in the region you pick, which helps with GDPR.

## 1. Create the server

**Cloud Console → your project → Add server**:

| Setting | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| Location | Closest to your users |
| Image | **Ubuntu 24.04** |
| Type | Shared vCPU (x86) with 2 GB+ RAM to start |
| Networking | **Public IPv4** on (Cipi needs one), IPv6 too |
| SSH key | Add yours |

## 2. Firewall (optional)

**Firewalls → Create**: inbound TCP 22, 80, 443 from any, applied to the server. Cipi also configures UFW and fail2ban on the host.

## 3. Install

```bash
$ ssh root@203.0.113.10
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
$ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10        # afterwards
```

## 4. DNS and first app

Create the `A`/`AAAA` records and follow [the main guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps) from step 4.

## Hetzner extras that fit

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Off-site backups | **Object Storage** (S3-compatible) as a `cipi backup` destination, in another location |
| More disk | Volumes for large uploads; keep `shared/` on fast local disk |
| A second server | Move or replicate apps with [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) |


## Cipi on Vultr, Akamai Linode, OVHcloud and Scaleway

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-vultr-linode-ovhcloud

Any provider works as long as you get a **full virtual machine** (KVM or similar) with **Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04**, a **public IPv4** and ports **22, 80 and 443** reachable. The installer checks the environment and stops with an explanation inside containers (LXC, OpenVZ).

| Provider | Create | Image | Firewall | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Vultr** | Deploy → Cloud Compute | Ubuntu 24.04 LTS x64 | Network → Firewall group (22, 80, 443) | Object Storage is S3-compatible for backups |
| **Akamai Linode** | Create → Linode | Ubuntu 24.04 LTS | Cloud Firewalls (22, 80, 443) | Object Storage is S3-compatible |
| **OVHcloud** | VPS or Public Cloud instance | Ubuntu 24.04 | Edge firewall / security groups | VPS images may log you in as `ubuntu`: run the installer with `sudo -i` |
| **Scaleway** | Instances → Create | Ubuntu 24.04 (Noble) | Security groups (22, 80, 443) | Object Storage is S3-compatible |

## Install

```bash
$ ssh root@203.0.113.10            # or ubuntu@… then: sudo -i
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

Then log in as `cipi` and follow [the main guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps) from step 4.

## Checklist for any provider

| Check | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Not a container product | Cipi manages the kernel firewall, swap and services |
| Public IPv4, not NAT-only | Let's Encrypt and visitors must reach the server |
| Reverse DNS set to your hostname | Helps deliverability of notification e-mail |
| Outbound 25 often blocked | Send mail through an SMTP provider on 587 |
| A second region or provider for backups | Point `cipi backup` at an S3-compatible bucket elsewhere |


## A Laravel API with a Next.js or Nuxt front end on one server

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-api-nextjs-nuxt

Two apps, one server: `api.acme.app` (Laravel) and `acme.app` (Next.js or Nuxt in SSR mode). Both deploy from Git with zero downtime; the Node app restarts blue/green.

```stack
acme.app | Node app, SSR, blue/green restarts
api.acme.app | Laravel app, FPM or Octane
Server | one Cipi install
```

## 1. The API

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=api --domain=api.acme.app \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/api.git --php=8.6
$ sudo cipi deploy api && sudo cipi ssl install api
```

For cookie-based auth from the front end, configure Sanctum: `SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS=acme.app`, `SESSION_DOMAIN=.acme.app`, and CORS for `https://acme.app`:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env api --set=SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS=acme.app
$ sudo cipi app env api --set=SESSION_DOMAIN=.acme.app
```

## 2. The front end

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=web --domain=acme.app \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/web.git --node=ssr --framework=next --node-version=24
$ sudo cipi deploy web && sudo cipi ssl install web
```

Use `--framework=nuxt` for Nuxt. Each deploy installs from your lockfile, builds, starts the new process, checks the health path and only then switches traffic.

| Mode | For |
| --- | --- |
| `ssr` | Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Remix, Astro SSR |
| `static` | Pre-rendered sites (Astro, `nuxt generate`) |
| `spa` | Vite single-page apps |

## 3. Point the front end at the API

Build-time variables go in the Node app's `shared/.env`, read at build:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env web --set=NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://api.acme.app
$ sudo cipi deploy web
```

## 4. Keep both in their repositories

Each repository can carry its own `cipi.yml`: workers, schedule and health for the API, `node:` settings for the front end. Examples in [cipi.yml recipes](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-recipes).


## CI/CD for Laravel with GitHub Actions or GitLab CI

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow

Push-to-deploy is great until a broken test reaches production. A pipeline adds the gate: test, optionally back up, deploy, and roll back if the deploy fails.

```flow
Push | to main
Test | php artisan test
Backup | optional
Deploy | ssh → cipi deploy
Roll back | on failure
```

## 1. A dedicated key for CI

```bash
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "ci-deploy" -f ~/.ssh/ci_deploy -N ""
$ cat ~/.ssh/ci_deploy.pub     # on the server: sudo cipi ssh add ""
$ cat ~/.ssh/ci_deploy         # → CI secret SERVER_SSH_KEY
```

Save `SERVER_SSH_KEY` and `SERVER_HOST` as repository secrets. Never reuse a personal key or the app's deploy key.

## 2. Turn the webhook off

So only the pipeline deploys. Remove the webhook from the repository settings, or recreate the app's webhook only when you need it again with `sudo cipi app webhook recreate shop`.

## 3. GitHub Actions

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: "8.6" }
      - run: composer install --no-interaction && cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate
      - run: php artisan test
  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SERVER_HOST }}
          username: cipi
          key: ${{ secrets.SERVER_SSH_KEY }}
          script: sudo cipi deploy shop || (sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback && exit 1)
```

## 4. GitLab CI

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages: [test, deploy]
test:
  stage: test
  image: php:8.6-cli
  script: [composer install, php artisan test]
deploy:
  stage: deploy
  only: [main]
  before_script:
    - eval $(ssh-agent -s) && echo "$SERVER_SSH_KEY" | tr -d '\r' | ssh-add -
    - mkdir -p ~/.ssh && ssh-keyscan -H $SERVER_HOST >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts
  script:
    - ssh cipi@$SERVER_HOST "sudo cipi deploy shop || (sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback && exit 1)"
```

## 5. Add a safety net

| Add | How |
| --- | --- |
| Database snapshot before migrations | `sudo cipi app edit shop --predeploy-snapshot` (every deploy) |
| Off-site backup step | `sudo cipi backup run --profile=shop-nightly` in a job before deploy |
| Validate `cipi.yml` | `php artisan cipi:yml validate --json` in the test job ([agent](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-yml)) |
| Automatic rollback when the app is down | A [health check](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks) with `rollback_on_unhealthy: true` |
| Alerts | `sudo cipi notification add slack …` ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts)) |

## Without SSH

Prefer HTTPS to SSH from CI? Use [cipi-cli](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client) with an API token that only has `deploy-manage`:

```bash
$ cipi-cli prod deploy shop
```

Next: a live URL for every branch with [preview environments](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-preview-environments).


## The self-hosted Laravel developer stack (2026)

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-developer-stack-2026

Every SaaS in a Laravel team's toolchain is reasonable on its own. Together they add up to a bill per developer, per server and per project, plus a pile of places where your data lives. Here's what's worth owning.

## What to own, what to buy

| Job | Self-hosted option | Bought option | Own it when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Server management and deploys | [Cipi](https://cipi.sh/) (free) | Forge, Ploi | Almost always: it's the part you run every day |
| Backups | `cipi backup` to any S3-compatible bucket | Panel add-ons | Always: you need them anyway |
| Search | Meilisearch on the server | Algolia | Index fits in RAM |
| Object storage | [Johnny](https://johnny.web.ap.it/), MinIO | S3, R2 | You have a second VPS |
| Error tracking and uptime | [Boogle](https://boogle.web.ap.it/) | Sentry, Flare, Better Stack | Error payloads contain personal data |
| Analytics | [IndieStats](https://indiestats.web.ap.it/) | Google Analytics, Plausible | You don't want consent banners |
| Transactional e-mail | — | Postmark, SES, Mailgun | Buy: deliverability is a full-time job |
| CI | — | GitHub Actions, GitLab CI | Buy: free tiers are generous |

## The cost math

The pattern that matters is **per-server pricing**. A server panel charged per server per month costs more every time you add a staging or client server, while the servers themselves keep getting cheaper. Self-hosting the panel turns that line into zero; the VPS bill stays the same either way.

What you pay instead is attention: updates, backups and security. That's why the self-hosted tool has to do those by itself: nightly PHP and nginx patches, verified backups, alerts. If it doesn't, the saving is an illusion.

## When SaaS still wins

| Situation | Why |
| --- | --- |
| No one on the team is comfortable on a server | A managed platform hides it |
| Autoscaling to zero matters more than cost | Serverless platforms do it better |
| Compliance requires a vendor's certifications | Buying them is cheaper than earning them |

## A sensible default

Own the server, the deploys, the backups and the data. Buy e-mail delivery and CI. Add self-hosted error tracking and analytics once you have a second server for them. Start with [Deploy Laravel on an Ubuntu VPS](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps).


## The Laravel ecosystem in 2026, mapped to production

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ecosystem-2026

Laravel is a framework plus a family of first-party and community tools. Choosing them is easy; running them in production is where projects stall. This map groups them by job and says what each needs from the server.

## Runtime

| Tool | Job | Needs on the server | On Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PHP-FPM | Classic request handling | A pool per app | Default |
| [Octane](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-octane-frankenphp) (FrankenPHP) | App kept in memory, much faster responses | A long-running process, a proxy | `--octane` |
| [Horizon](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues) | Queues with a dashboard | Redis, a supervised process | `cipi worker horizon enable` |
| Queue workers | Background jobs | Supervisor | One per app by default |
| Scheduler | Cron-like tasks | One cron line | Built in |
| [Reverb](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-reverb-websockets) | WebSockets | A process, a WebSocket proxy, open-file limits | `cipi app reverb enable` |

## Data and search

| Tool | Job | On Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MariaDB / MySQL | Default relational store | Default |
| PostgreSQL | JSONB, extensions, analytics | `cipi db install pgsql` |
| Valkey (Redis) | Cache, sessions, queues for Horizon | Included |
| [Scout + Meilisearch](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-scout-meilisearch) | Full-text search | `cipi search install` |

## UI

| Tool | Good for |
| --- | --- |
| Blade + Livewire | Full-stack reactive apps in PHP |
| Filament | Admin panels and back offices |
| Inertia (Vue, React, Svelte) | SPA feel with Laravel routing |
| Vite | Asset builds, run on deploy with `node_build` |

## Quality and observability

| Tool | Job |
| --- | --- |
| Pest / PHPUnit | Tests; run them in [CI before deploying](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow) |
| Larastan, Pint, Rector | Static analysis, style, upgrades |
| Pulse | Performance overview inside the app |
| Telescope | Local and staging debugging (off in production) |
| Health checks | `/up` and the [agent's `/cipi/health`](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-health-monitoring) |

## Hosting choices

You can rent all of this as a managed platform, rent a dashboard to manage your own VPS, or run it yourself for free. That trade-off is the subject of [our comparisons](https://cipi.sh/alternatives); the [developer stack guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-developer-stack-2026) does the cost math.


## Laravel queues and Horizon in production

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues

Every Laravel app on Cipi starts with one worker on the `default` queue, under Supervisor. This guide adds queues, scales them, and switches to Horizon when you want a dashboard.

## 1. Add and scale queues

```bash
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=emails --processes=3
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=exports --processes=1 --timeout=7200
$ sudo cipi worker edit shop --queue=default --processes=2
$ sudo cipi worker list shop
```

| Flag | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--queue` | Queue to consume | `default` |
| `--processes` | Parallel processes | 1 |
| `--timeout` | Seconds before a job is killed | 60 |

Dispatch to a queue as usual: `SendInvoice::dispatch($order)->onQueue('emails')`.

## 2. Switch to Horizon

Horizon needs the queues on Redis. Each app has [Valkey](https://cipi.sh/docs/valkey), a drop-in Redis, ready:

```bash
$ composer require laravel/horizon && php artisan horizon:install   # commit, deploy
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis
$ sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop
```

Horizon replaces the app's `queue:work` workers. Configure supervisors per queue in `config/horizon.php`. Protect the dashboard with the `viewHorizon` gate.

When a deploy finds Horizon installed and queues on Redis with no worker, it enables Horizon for you; it never overrides a choice you made.

## 3. Deploys don't break jobs

```flow
Stop workers | before the swap
Swap release | atomic
Restart workers | on the new code
```

Workers never run old code against a migrated database. Long jobs: set `--timeout` above the job's duration so a deploy doesn't kill them mid-run.

## 4. In cipi.yml

```yaml
workers:
  horizon: false
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 2 }
    - { queue: emails, processes: 3, tries: 5, timeout: 300 }
```

Or `horizon: true` to hand everything to Horizon. [More on cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml).


## Laravel Octane with FrankenPHP on your own server

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-octane-frankenphp

[Laravel Octane](https://laravel.com/docs/octane) boots your app once and keeps it in memory, so each request skips the framework bootstrap. With FrankenPHP as the server, a typical app answers several times faster on the same hardware. Cipi runs it natively, without containers, next to your PHP-FPM apps.

## 1. Prepare the project

```bash
$ composer require laravel/octane
$ php artisan octane:install --server=frankenphp
```

Commit both changes. Octane apps keep state between requests: avoid storing per-request data in static properties or singletons. The [Octane docs](https://laravel.com/docs/octane#dependency-injection-and-octane) list the patterns to watch.

## 2. Create the app as Octane, or convert one

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/shop.git --octane
$ sudo cipi deploy shop
```

An existing app moves over (and back) in one command; the certificate is kept:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app convert shop --to=octane
$ sudo cipi app convert shop --to=fpm
```

## 3. What runs on the server

```flow
Nginx | static files, TLS
Octane on 127.0.0.1 | a port in 8100–8999
FrankenPHP build | pinned for this app
Supervisor | restarts, reloads on deploy
```

| Piece | Setting |
| --- | --- |
| Nginx | Serves `current/public` directly and proxies the rest to the app's local port |
| Process | Supervisor program `shop-octane`, next to the queue workers |
| `.env` | `OCTANE_SERVER=frankenphp`, `OCTANE_HTTPS=true` |
| Deploys | The pinned binary is linked into the new release, then Octane reloads |

## 4. Tune the workers

```bash
$ sudo cipi app limits shop --octane-workers=4
```

Start with one worker per CPU core and watch memory with `sudo cipi status`. Long jobs belong on [queues or Horizon](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues), WebSockets on [Reverb](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-reverb-websockets).

## 5. Keep FrankenPHP patched, safely

```bash
$ sudo cipi frankenphp              # each app's build and PHP, patched or not
$ sudo cipi frankenphp upgrade shop  # newest build on the same PHP minor
```

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Upgrades stay on the app's PHP minor | No surprise PHP jump |
| Octane must answer after an upgrade | Otherwise the previous build comes back |
| Nightly patches via `cipi autoupdate` | Security fixes without manual work |

To move to a new PHP minor: `sudo cipi app edit shop --php=8.6`, then `sudo cipi frankenphp upgrade shop`.

## In cipi.yml

The runtime is chosen at creation or with `convert`; worker counts can live in the repository:

```yaml
app:
  limits: { octane_workers: 4 }
```


## Preview environments for every Laravel branch

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-preview-environments

Reviewers click a link instead of pulling a branch. Each preview is a complete, isolated Cipi app at `feature-x-shop-3a1f9c2e.preview.example.com`, removed when the branch is deleted.

```flow
Push feature/x | any branch but main
CI computes a name | stable per branch
Create or deploy | cipi app create / deploy
Live URL | on the wildcard domain
Branch deleted | app deleted
```

## 1. One-time setup

| Step | How |
| --- | --- |
| Wildcard DNS | `A *.preview.example.com → server IP` |
| Wildcard certificate | DNS-01 with Cloudflare: see [wildcard domains](https://cipi.sh/docs/wildcard-domains) |
| Repository access | A read-only token so previews need no deploy key per app |
| CI secrets | `SERVER_HOST`, `SERVER_SSH_KEY`, `DEPLOY_WILDCARD_DOMAIN` |

## 2. The script and the workflow

The complete, copy-paste versions of `.cipi/preview.sh` and `.github/workflows/preview.yml` are in the [preview environments docs](https://cipi.sh/docs/preview-environments). The idea:

```bash
# up: create once, deploy every push
cipi app show "$APP" &>/dev/null || cipi app create --user="$APP" --domain="$DOMAIN" \
    --repository="$REPO" --branch="$BRANCH"
cipi deploy "$APP"
# down: when the branch is deleted
cipi app delete "$APP" --force
```

The app name is a short hash of branch and repository, so it's stable for the branch and never collides.

## 3. Make previews useful

| Add | How |
| --- | --- |
| Realistic data without personal data | Import an [anonymized dump](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps) after create |
| A login in front | `basic_auth` in `cipi-preview.yml`, with `--env=preview` on create |
| Fewer resources | One worker, no backups, in the same file |
| A link in the pull request | Post `https://$DOMAIN` as a PR comment from the workflow |

## 4. Clean up

The workflow's `delete` trigger removes the app. Check for leftovers now and then with `sudo cipi app list`.


## Real-time Laravel with Reverb, on your own domain

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-reverb-websockets

[Laravel Reverb](https://reverb.laravel.com) is Laravel's own WebSocket server. Here you'll add live notifications to an app and run Reverb in production on the same domain and certificate as the app: no Pusher account, no extra port to open, no credentials to invent.

## 1. Add broadcasting to the project

```bash
$ composer require laravel/reverb
$ php artisan install:broadcasting
```

That installs Echo and writes `resources/js/echo.js`. Broadcast an event:

```php
class OrderShipped implements ShouldBroadcast
{
    public function __construct(public Order $order) {}

    public function broadcastOn(): array
    {
        return [new PrivateChannel('orders.'.$this->order->user_id)];
    }
}
```

```js
Echo.private(`orders.${userId}`).listen('OrderShipped', (e) => {
    toast(`Order ${e.order.number} shipped`);
});
```

Commit and push.

## 2. Turn Reverb on for the app

```bash
$ sudo cipi app reverb enable shop
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop       # wss:// instead of ws://
$ sudo cipi deploy shop             # Vite bakes VITE_REVERB_* into the bundle
```

```flow
Browser | wss://shop.example.com/app/{key}
Nginx | same domain, same certificate
Reverb on 127.0.0.1 | a port in 9000–9099
Supervisor | shop-reverb, as the app user
```

Cipi generates the `REVERB_*` credentials once, writes the `VITE_REVERB_*` copies for the front end, and proxies only the WebSocket paths. The stock `echo.js` reads exactly those variables.

## 3. Check it

```bash
$ sudo cipi app reverb status shop
 Reverb: enabled 127.0.0.1:9000
 shop-reverb RUNNING pid 21847, uptime 3 days
 Clients dial: wss://shop.example.com:443/app/3f9c1ab27de40518b6c4
```

Events are broadcast from queued jobs, so keep a [worker or Horizon](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues) running.

| Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Clients use `ws://` after adding a certificate | `cipi app reverb enable shop` again, then deploy |
| `Missing in .env` in status | Run `enable` again: it fills in missing keys, keeps port and credentials |
| Domain changed | Redeploy so the bundle picks up the new host |

## 4. Keep it in the repository

```yaml
# cipi.yml
workers:
  reverb: true
```

A clone or staging copy gets its own port, credentials and host, never production's.


## Laravel Scout with Meilisearch, self-hosted

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-scout-meilisearch

Here you'll add instant, typo-tolerant product search to a Laravel shop with [Scout](https://laravel.com/docs/scout) and [Meilisearch](https://www.meilisearch.com), running on the same server. Each app gets a key that can only touch its own indexes.

## 1. Install Meilisearch on the server

```bash
$ sudo cipi search install
```

A single binary under systemd, listening on localhost, with a hardened unit and a health check. The master key lives in a root-only file.

## 2. Prepare the model

```bash
$ composer require laravel/scout meilisearch/meilisearch-php http-interop/http-factory-guzzle
$ php artisan vendor:publish --provider="Laravel\Scout\ScoutServiceProvider"
```

```php
use Laravel\Scout\Searchable;

class Product extends Model
{
    use Searchable;

    public function toSearchableArray(): array
    {
        return [
            'id' => $this->id,
            'name' => $this->name,
            'brand' => $this->brand,
            'price' => $this->price,
        ];
    }
}
```

Filterable and sortable attributes go in `config/scout.php` under `meilisearch.index-settings`. Commit and deploy.

## 3. Enable search for the app

```bash
$ sudo cipi search enable shop
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop scout:sync-index-settings
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop scout:import "App\Models\Product"
```

Cipi writes `SCOUT_DRIVER=meilisearch`, the host, a key scoped to `shop-*` indexes and the prefix into the app's `.env`.

```flow
App shop | SCOUT_PREFIX=shop-
Scoped key | shop-* indexes only
Meilisearch | 127.0.0.1, no public port
```

## 4. Search

```php
$results = Product::search($request->q)
    ->where('brand', 'Acme')
    ->paginate(20);
```

Add `scout:sync-index-settings` to your deploy steps so settings follow the code:

```yaml
# cipi.yml
search: true
deploy:
  post:
    - artisan scout:sync-index-settings
```

## Operations

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Status and keys | `sudo cipi search status --check`, `sudo cipi search list` |
| Rotate the app key | `sudo cipi search key rotate shop` (`.env` updated) |
| Upgrade | `sudo cipi search upgrade` (old binary returns if the store is refused) |
| Turn off for an app | `sudo cipi search disable shop --purge-indexes` |


## Zero-downtime Laravel deploys with safe migrations

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-zero-downtime-migrations

Zero downtime is two problems: switching code without a gap, and changing the database without breaking the code that's still live. Cipi solves the first. This guide shows how to handle the second.

## How a release goes live

```flow
Clone | new folder in releases/
Build | composer, npm, link .env and storage
Migrate | against the live database
Swap | one atomic symlink
Restart | workers, Octane, FPM reload
```

The old release keeps serving until the swap. The previous five releases stay on disk for an instant `sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback`.

## The catch: migrations run before the swap

For a few seconds the **old code runs against the new schema**. Migrations must be backward compatible with the release that's still live.

| Change | Safe way |
| --- | --- |
| Add a column | Nullable or with a default. Safe in one deploy |
| Rename a column | Add the new column, write to both, backfill, switch reads, drop the old one in a later deploy |
| Drop a column | First deploy code that no longer uses it, then drop it in the next deploy |
| Add an index on a big table | Use the engine's online method (`ALGORITHM=INPLACE` on MariaDB, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on PostgreSQL) |
| Make a column NOT NULL | Backfill first, constrain later |

This "expand, then contract" rhythm is what lets you deploy many times a day.

## Take a snapshot first

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --snapshot             # dump first, continue if the dump fails
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --snapshot-required    # abort the deploy if the dump fails
$ sudo cipi app edit shop --predeploy-snapshot # every deploy, whatever triggered it
```

Dumps land in `/var/log/cipi/backups/`. To undo a bad migration:

```bash
$ sudo cipi db restore shop /var/log/cipi/backups/shop_20261123_143012.sql.gz
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback
```

## Roll back automatically

```yaml
# cipi.yml
health:
  url: "https://shop.example.com/up"
  expect: 200
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true
deploy:
  predeploy_snapshot: true
```

After every deploy Cipi calls the health URL. If the new release doesn't answer as expected, the previous release goes back live and you get notified.

## Know who deployed what

Every deploy, from any trigger, is recorded in a hash-chained [audit trail](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit):

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --audit
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --history
```


## cipi.yml recipes for common Laravel setups

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-recipes

Start from the recipe closest to your app, run `php artisan cipi:yml validate`, commit, then `sudo cipi yml plan ` after the deploy. Every key is documented in the [reference](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml).

## SaaS: Horizon, Reverb, search, backups

```yaml
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.6"
  aliases: ["www.acme.app"]
  www: to-root
workers:
  horizon: true
  reverb: true
schedule: true
search: true
health:
  url: "https://acme.app/up"
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true
deploy:
  predeploy_snapshot: true
  node_build: "npm ci && npm run build"
  post:
    - artisan scout:sync-index-settings
env: { required: [STRIPE_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET, POSTMARK_TOKEN] }
backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: acme-db, scope: db, every: 30m, keep: 48, destinations: [local] }
    - { name: acme-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 2 * * *", keep_days: 30, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

## API on Octane, extra database, queues

```yaml
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.6"
  limits: { octane_workers: 4 }
databases:
  - name: api_reporting
    engine: pgsql
workers:
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 2 }
    - { queue: webhooks, processes: 4, tries: 10, timeout: 120 }
schedule: true
crons:
  - { every: 30m, run: artisan queue:prune-batches }
```

## Multi-tenant on a wildcard domain

```yaml
version: 1
app:
  aliases: ["*.acme.app"]
ssl: { force_https: true }
health:
  url: "https://www.acme.app/up"
```

Wildcard certificates use DNS-01: see [wildcard domains](https://cipi.sh/docs/wildcard-domains).

## Marketing site moved: redirects and a proxied blog

```yaml
version: 1
redirects:
  - { from: /pricing-old, to: /pricing }
  - { from: /docs/, to: "https://docs.acme.app/", code: 308 }
proxies:
  - { prefix: /blog/, upstream: "http://127.0.0.1:3000", strip_prefix: true }
```

## Next.js front end (Node app)

```yaml
version: 1
node:
  framework: next
  mode: ssr
  version: 24
deploy:
  branch: main
```

## Staging overrides

```yaml
# cipi-staging.yml
version: 1
app:
  basic_auth: { users: [preview] }
workers:
  queues: [{ queue: default, processes: 1 }]
deploy: { branch: develop, predeploy_snapshot: false }
```


## Staging and production from one repository with cipi.yml

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-staging-production

One repository, two apps: `shop` (production, branch `main`) and `shop-stg` (staging, branch `develop`). Each reads its own file, so staging can run fewer workers, skip backups and keep basic auth on, without a single `if` in your deploy scripts.

```stack
Repository | cipi.yml + cipi-staging.yml
shop | env production → reads cipi.yml
shop-stg | env staging → reads cipi-staging.yml
```

## 1. Clone production as staging

```bash
$ sudo cipi app clone shop --domain=staging.shop.example.com --name=shop-stg --env=staging
```

The clone gets its own user, database, PHP pool, credentials and deploy key. It never shares production's secrets.

## 2. Add the staging file

```yaml
# cipi-staging.yml
version: 1
app:
  basic_auth:
    users: [preview]          # password set once on the server
workers:
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 1 }
schedule: true
deploy:
  branch: develop
  predeploy_snapshot: false
```

Keep `cipi.yml` for production. An app reads `cipi-.yml` first, then falls back to `cipi.yml`.

## 3. Plan and apply on staging

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop-stg
$ sudo cipi yml plan shop-stg      # deploy branch: main → develop (from the next deploy)
$ sudo cipi yml apply shop-stg
$ sudo cipi yml auto shop-stg on
```

From now on, pushes to `develop` deploy staging and pushes to `main` deploy production.

## Rules that keep production safe

| Rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| The server sets the environment (`--env`), not the file | A commit can't make production read the staging file |
| An invalid `cipi-staging.yml` doesn't fall back to `cipi.yml` | Errors are explicit, never silent |
| Staging data is never production's | Clones get new credentials; use the [anonymizer](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps) for realistic data |

Want a URL per branch instead of one staging app? See [preview environments](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-preview-environments).


## cipi.yml: keep your server settings in the repository

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml

Most panels keep an app's server settings in a database you can't review. Cipi lets you put them in **`cipi.yml`**, a file at the root of your repository. It travels with each release: you review it in a pull request, see exactly what it would change, and apply it in one step.

```flow
Commit cipi.yml | reviewed like code
Deploy | the file ships with the release
Plan | every change listed first
Apply | all or nothing
```

## 1. Start from what the app already has

```bash
$ sudo cipi yml generate shop --save
$ cat /home/shop/cipi.yml
```

Commit that file at the root of the repository. After the next deploy, `cipi yml plan shop` should say there's nothing to do: the file describes the server as it is.

## 2. Describe the app

A typical Laravel app:

```yaml
version: 1

app:
  php: "8.6"
  aliases: ["www.shop.example.com"]
  www: to-root
  ini: { upload_max_filesize: 50M }

workers:
  horizon: true
  reverb: true

schedule: true
search: true

health:
  url: "https://shop.example.com/up"
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true

deploy:
  branch: main
  predeploy_snapshot: true
  node_build: "npm ci && npm run build"
  post:
    - artisan cache:clear

env: { required: [STRIPE_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET, MAIL_HOST] }

backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: shop-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 2 * * *", keep_days: 14, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

| Block | Replaces |
| --- | --- |
| `app` | `cipi php`, `cipi alias`, `cipi www`, `cipi ini`, `cipi app limits` |
| `workers`, `schedule` | `cipi worker`, `cipi app reverb`, the scheduler cron |
| `search` | `cipi search enable` |
| `health` | `cipi health set` |
| `deploy` | `cipi deploy-config` |
| `backup.profiles` | `cipi backup profile` |

The full list, with routes, proxies, crons and Node apps, is in the [cipi.yml reference](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml).

## 3. Validate before you push

Install the [Cipi Agent](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent) in the app and validate with the same rules as the server, locally or in CI:

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent
$ php artisan cipi:yml validate
```

Add `# yaml-language-server: $schema=./cipi.schema.json` at the top of the file (after `php artisan cipi:yml schema --write`) for autocompletion in VS Code or PhpStorm.

## 4. Plan and apply

After deploying the release that contains the file:

`plan` lists every change and every blocker. `apply` performs them as one transaction: if anything fails, nothing is left half done.

## 5. Apply on every deploy

```bash
$ sudo cipi yml auto shop on
```

From now on each successful deploy (CLI, webhook or panel) applies the file. **Anyone who can push can now change this app's server settings**, which is the point: protect the branch and review the file like code.

## Why it's safe

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Plan before apply | You see every change; blockers stop everything |
| Namespaced resources | Databases must be `shop` or `shop_*`, backup profiles `shop` or `shop-*`: a file can't touch another app |
| No secrets | Required variables are names; credentials are written to `shared/`, never to the repo |
| Allowlisted commands | `deploy.post` and `crons` accept known runners only (`artisan`, `php`, `composer`, `npm`…) |
| Server picks the file | The app's environment decides between `cipi.yml` and `cipi-staging.yml`; a commit can't redirect production |

Next: one repository, two servers or two apps, with [staging and production files](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-staging-production).


## GDPR-safe production data for developers with the Cipi anonymizer

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps

Debugging with fake seed data misses the bugs that real data causes. Copying production to laptops is a GDPR problem. The anonymizer in [Cipi Agent](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-laravel-mcp) gives you the middle ground: production's structure and volume, with every personal field replaced.

```flow
Request | cipi-cli or POST /cipi/db
Dump | mysqldump / pg_dump
Rewrite | only the listed columns
E-mail | signed link, 15 minutes
```

## 1. Enable it in the app

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent                    # commit, deploy
$ php artisan cipi:service anonymize --enable    # as the app user
$ php artisan cipi:generate-token anonymize
$ php artisan cipi:init-anonymize --scan
```

`--scan` reads your schema and proposes a transformation for every column that looks personal (e-mails, names, phones, addresses, IPs, tokens, passwords, tax ids, card data, free text) and empties tables like `sessions`, `jobs` and `password_reset_tokens`. The file goes to `~/.db/anonymization.json`, **outside the repository**.

## 2. Review the rules

```json
{
  "transformations": {
    "users": {
      "name": "fakeName",
      "email": { "type": "fakeEmail", "consistent": true },
      "password": "password",
      "phone": "mask:3,2"
    },
    "orders": {
      "customer_email": { "type": "fakeEmail", "consistent": true },
      "internal_notes": "fakeParagraph"
    }
  },
  "truncate": ["sessions", "jobs", "failed_jobs", "password_reset_tokens"],
  "options": { "faker_locale": "it_IT", "consistent": true, "seed": "keep-this-private" }
}
```

Every password becomes the hash of `options.password` (default `password`), so developers can log in. Then audit against the live schema:

```bash
$ php artisan cipi:anonymize-audit
```

It fails on unknown tables or columns and lists personal-looking columns you didn't cover. **Run it after every migration.**

## 3. Get a dump from your laptop

```bash
$ cipi-cli prod db anonymize shop --email dev@example.com
✓ Anonymization job queued for 'shop'
$ cipi-cli db anonymize download "" -o - | mysql -u root shop_local
```

No SSH, no token in your shell history: [cipi-cli](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client) reads it through the API. The link expires after 15 minutes.

## 4. Check it

```bash
$ grep -c "real.customer@gmail.com" shop.sql     # must be 0
```

## Good practice

| Do | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Use `consistent` with a private `seed` | Data stays joinable; fakes can't be reversed |
| Never commit `anonymization.json` | It maps your schema |
| Rotate the token when people leave | `cipi:generate-token anonymize` |
| Give AI assistants the dump, not production | Same bugs, no personal data |

Full reference: [Database anonymizer](https://cipi.sh/docs/anonymizer).


## Monitor a Laravel app's health with the Cipi Agent and any uptime service

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-health-monitoring

Laravel's `/up` route says the app boots. The agent's `/cipi/health` says whether the app actually works: database, cache, queue, storage and the deploy.

## 1. Enable the endpoint

```bash
$ php artisan cipi:service health --enable
$ php artisan cipi:generate-token health
$ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CIPI_HEALTH_TOKEN" https://shop.example.com/cipi/health
```

```json
{
  "status": "healthy",
  "checks": {
    "database": { "ok": true, "driver": "mysql" },
    "cache": { "ok": true, "driver": "database" },
    "queue": { "ok": true, "pending_jobs": 0, "failed_jobs": 0 },
    "storage": { "ok": true, "disk_free_gb": 31.2, "disk_used_percent": 41 },
    "deploy": { "ok": true, "short_commit": "0123456", "in_progress": false }
  }
}
```

If the database, cache, queue or storage fails, `status` becomes `degraded` with **HTTP 503**, which is what uptime services watch.

## 2. Connect an uptime service

| Service | Set up |
| --- | --- |
| Better Stack, UptimeRobot, Pingdom | HTTP monitor on `/cipi/health`, header `Authorization: Bearer `, alert on non-200 |
| Grafana / Prometheus | Blackbox exporter with the header; parse `checks.*.ok` with a JSON exporter |
| Plain cron | `curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer …" https://…/cipi/health >/dev/null || notify` |

## 3. Combine with the server checks

| Layer | Watches | Alerts via |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cipi monitor` | CPU, memory, disk, services, certificates | Your [Cipi channels](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts) |
| `cipi health` | One URL per app, every 5 minutes and after deploys; can roll back | Your Cipi channels |
| `/cipi/health` | Inside the app: DB, cache, queue, storage, deploy | Your uptime service, from outside |

The outside view catches what the server can't see about itself: DNS, network, a down server.


## Cipi Agent: connect your Laravel app to its server

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-laravel-mcp

`cipi/agent` is a Laravel package that lets your app talk to the server it runs on. One `composer require` and the app gains five features, each behind its own token and each off until you want it.

| Feature | Endpoint / command | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Push-to-deploy | `POST /cipi/webhook` | [Webhook deploys](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-webhook-deploy) |
| Health | `GET /cipi/health` | [Uptime monitoring](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-health-monitoring) |
| MCP for AI assistants | `/cipi/mcp` | [Claude, Cursor and the Cipi MCP](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents) |
| `cipi.yml` tooling | `php artisan cipi:yml` | [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml) |
| Anonymized dumps | `php artisan cipi:anonymize`, `/cipi/db` | [Safe data for developers](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps) |

## 1. Install

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent
$ git commit -am "Add Cipi Agent" && git push
```

On a Cipi server, `cipi app create` already wrote the `.env` variables; the service provider auto-discovers. Laravel 12 or 13, PHP 8.3+.

## 2. Check it after the deploy

```bash
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop cipi:status
```

`cipi:status` shows configuration, environment, live release and commit, enabled features, `cipi.yml` validity and database connectivity.

## 3. Turn on what you need

```bash
$ php artisan cipi:service health --enable && php artisan cipi:generate-token health
$ php artisan cipi:service mcp --enable && php artisan cipi:generate-token mcp
$ php artisan cipi:service anonymize --enable && php artisan cipi:generate-token anonymize
```

Run them as the app user (`ssh shop@server`) or through `sudo cipi app artisan shop …`. Each feature has its own token; a disabled feature answers **404**, so it's invisible.

## 4. Use it in CI

```yaml
- run: php artisan cipi:yml validate --json --app=shop
```

The agent ships the same `cipi.yml` validator as the server, so a broken file fails the pipeline instead of the deploy.

## Agent or API?

The agent works **inside one app**, on its domain. The [Cipi API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) runs on its own domain and manages the **whole server**. Install the [PHP SDK](https://cipi.sh/docs/php-sdk) next to the agent and the app's MCP gains server-side tools: rollback, database backup, job status.


## Push-to-deploy Laravel from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Gitea

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-webhook-deploy

With a token, Cipi sets up the webhook on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps by itself. This guide shows what happens behind it, and how to wire Gitea or Forgejo by hand.

```flow
git push | to the deploy branch
Webhook | POST /cipi/webhook, signed
Verify | signature, branch
Trigger file | instant HTTP answer
Deploy | within a minute, as the app user
```

The request never runs the deploy itself: it verifies the push and drops a trigger. A cron picks it up and deploys with zero downtime. A slow build can't time out a webhook, and a forged request can't start anything.

## 1. Get the URL and token

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --webhook
```

## 2. Add the webhook

| Provider | Payload URL | Secret / token | Events |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub | `https://shop.example.com/cipi/webhook` | Secret = token (HMAC-SHA256), content type JSON | Just the push event |
| GitLab | same | Secret token | Push events |
| Bitbucket Cloud | same | Secret (HMAC) | Repository push |
| Gitea / Forgejo | same | Secret (HMAC) | Push events |

Only pushes to the app's branch (`CIPI_DEPLOY_BRANCH`) deploy; others answer `skipped`. GitHub's ping answers `pong`.

## 3. Push and watch

```bash
$ git push origin main
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --status      # running, queued or idle
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --log
```

## 4. Know who pushed

Each trigger records what the push claimed (provider, pusher, commit, delivery ID, IP) in the [deploy audit](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit). It's recorded as a claim, not a fact: the ledger is hash-chained, so it can't be quietly edited later.

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --audit
```

## Rotate the secret

```bash
$ sudo cipi app webhook recreate shop --rotate-secret
```

Need tests before deploying? Turn the webhook off and use [a pipeline](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow).


## Manage Laravel in production with Claude, Cursor and the Cipi MCP

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents

MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets an AI assistant call tools. Cipi ships two MCP servers, so you can ask *"is production healthy, what failed last night, deploy main"* and get answers from the real app, not guesses.

| | Agent MCP | Server MCP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Endpoint | `https://shop.example.com/cipi/mcp` | `https://api.example.com/mcp` |
| Scope | One app: health, logs, database, Artisan, deploy, `cipi.yml` | The server: apps, domains, SSL, databases, backups, PHP |
| Installed with | `composer require cipi/agent` | `cipi api api.example.com` |

## 1. Turn on the agent's MCP server

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent        # commit, push, deploy
# as the app user on the server (or: sudo cipi app artisan shop …)
$ php artisan cipi:service mcp --enable
$ php artisan cipi:generate-token mcp
$ php artisan cipi:mcp               # endpoint + ready-to-paste config
```

## 2. Connect your assistant

```bash
# Claude Code
$ claude mcp add --transport http cipi-shop https://shop.example.com/cipi/mcp \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_CIPI_MCP_TOKEN"
```

```json
// Cursor: ~/.cursor/mcp.json
{ "mcpServers": { "cipi-shop": {
    "type": "http", "url": "https://shop.example.com/cipi/mcp",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_CIPI_MCP_TOKEN" } } } }
```

VS Code and Claude Desktop configs are in the [MCP docs](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp#clients). VS Code can prompt for the token so it's never committed.

## 3. Ask real questions

```text
You:    Is production healthy, and what commit is live?
Claude: [health, deploy_status] Healthy. Release 20261109103000, commit 0123456 (webhook, 42 s).
You:    Show the last errors and tell me which job fails.
Claude: [logs level=error] InvoiceJob: column invoices.paid_at not found.
        [artisan migrate:status] 2026_11_08_add_paid_at is pending.
You:    Deploy main and note that Jane asked.
Claude: [deploy actor=jane@example.com] Queued; it runs within a minute.
```

| Tool | What it's good for |
| --- | --- |
| `health`, `deploy_status` | "Is it up? What's live? Is a deploy running?" |
| `logs` | Laravel, Nginx, PHP, worker, Horizon, Reverb and deploy logs with level and keyword filters |
| `db_schema`, `db_query` | Understand data; reads capped at 100 rows |
| `artisan` | `migrate:status`, `queue:retry`, cache commands; dangerous ones blocked |
| `env_check`, `cipi_yml` | Missing variables; validate a `cipi.yml` draft before you commit it |
| `deploy` | Queue a zero-downtime deploy, recorded in the audit with who asked |

## 4. Add the server MCP

For server work ("create a staging app", "issue the certificate", "back up the database"), install the API on its own domain and create a token with `mcp-access`:

```bash
$ sudo cipi api api.example.com
$ sudo cipi api token create --name=claude --abilities=mcp-access
$ claude mcp add --transport http cipi-server https://api.example.com/mcp \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer "
```

Destructive host operations (dropping databases, removing PHP versions, installing software) are kept off the API on purpose.

## Guardrails in one table

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| One token per feature | Rotate with `php artisan cipi:generate-token mcp`; disabled routes answer 404 |
| SQL and Artisan guards | No DDL, no `GRANT`, no `migrate:fresh`, no `tinker` |
| Redaction | Secrets masked in every output |
| Origin check | Browser requests from other hosts refused |
| Tool annotations | Clients know which tools are read-only and ask before acting |
| Audit | Deploys record the actor in the [hash-chained ledger](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit) |

> [!tip] For production, start with `CIPI_MCP_DB_WRITE=false`. Need realistic data for the assistant to experiment on? Give it an [anonymized dump](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps) instead of production.


## Spec-driven development with AI agents in Laravel

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/spec-driven-development-ai-laravel

AI coding agents are good at implementing a clear, testable specification and bad at guessing what you meant. The teams getting value write the spec first, keep the agent inside guardrails, and give it eyes on production through MCP.

```flow
Spec | what and why, acceptance criteria
Tests | written from the spec
Agent | implements until tests pass
Review | a human, on a preview URL
Production | deploy, then observe through MCP
```

## 1. Write the spec, not the prompt

| A good spec has | Example |
| --- | --- |
| The user and the problem | "Accountants can't find unpaid invoices quickly" |
| Acceptance criteria | "Filter by status and due date; overdue rows highlighted" |
| Constraints | "No new tables; reuse `invoices.paid_at`" |
| Out of scope | "No export in this iteration" |

Tools like [Larapilot](https://larapilot.web.ap.it/) structure this with personas and review steps on top of Laravel Boost.

## 2. Tests before code

Ask the agent to write Pest tests from the acceptance criteria first, review them, then let it implement until they pass. The tests are the contract.

## 3. Review on a real URL

Push the branch and get a [preview environment](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-preview-environments). Reviewers click instead of pulling code; seed it with an [anonymized dump](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps) so edge cases from real data show up.

## 4. Close the loop on production

After the deploy, the same assistant can check the result through the [Cipi MCP](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents):

```text
You:    Did the invoices release go out cleanly? Any new errors since?
Claude: [deploy_status] Release 134 live, 58 s, from the pipeline.
        [logs level=error since=deploy] None.
```

## Guardrails that matter

| Risk | Guardrail |
| --- | --- |
| Agent runs destructive SQL | MCP SQL guard blocks DDL and multi-statements; `CIPI_MCP_DB_WRITE=false` |
| Agent sees personal data | Redaction in outputs; anonymized dumps for experiments |
| Agent deploys untested code | Deploy only through CI with tests; the MCP `deploy` tool records who asked |
| Server config drifts | `cipi.yml` changes go through pull requests like code |


## Put a Laravel server behind Cloudflare Zero Trust

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel

With a Cloudflare Tunnel the server dials out to Cloudflare, and visitors reach it through Cloudflare's network. Once every app goes through the tunnel, you can close ports 80, 443 and even 22. Cipi does it in reversible steps; nothing closes until you ask.

```flow
Token | Tunnel, Access, DNS
Enable | tunnel; ports still open
Route | apps, panel, SSH
Test | from your laptop
Lock | close the ports
```

## 1. Create an API token

In Cloudflare: **My Profile → API Tokens → Create**, with Account · Cloudflare Tunnel: Edit, Account · Access: Apps and Policies: Edit, Zone · DNS: Edit (and Zone · SSL and Certificates for Origin CA certificates).

```bash
$ sudo cipi zt token set --token=CF_API_TOKEN --account=ACCOUNT_ID
$ sudo cipi zt enable
```

`enable` installs `cloudflared`, creates the tunnel and teaches Nginx, fail2ban and CrowdSec Cloudflare's IP ranges (refreshed daily). **No port is closed yet.**

## 2. Route the apps

```bash
$ sudo cipi zt hostname add shop          # public, through CDN and WAF
$ sudo cipi zt hostname add shop-stg
$ sudo cipi zt access enable shop-stg     # login required (Cloudflare Access)
$ sudo cipi zt access enable --gui        # the web panel too
```

Access protects staging and the panel with your identity provider. `/cipi/webhook` stays reachable so pushes still deploy.

## 3. SSH through the tunnel

```bash
$ sudo cipi zt ssh enable --hostname=ssh.example.com
```

On your laptop:

```text
# ~/.ssh/config
Host ssh.example.com
  ProxyCommand cloudflared access ssh --hostname %h
  User cipi
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
```

Test `ssh ssh.example.com` **before** the next step.

## 4. Certificates

A closed origin can't renew over HTTP. Move each app to DNS validation, or use a long-lived Cloudflare Origin CA certificate:

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop --dns=cloudflare
```

## 5. Close the ports

```bash
$ sudo cipi zt lock http --yes     # 80/443 closed, or Cloudflare-only
$ sudo cipi zt lock ssh --yes      # 22 closed; SSH only through Access
$ sudo cipi zt status
```

> [!warning] Lock SSH only after SSH through the tunnel works from your machine, and keep your provider's web console handy. Deploys aren't affected: they run locally.

Every step has its undo: `unlock http`, `ssh unlock`, `access disable`, `hostname remove`, `disable`.


## Laravel production security checklist

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-security-checklist

Security on your own server is a list of boring things done every time. Here's the list, split between what's yours (the app) and what the server should do for you.

## The app

| Check | How |
| --- | --- |
| `APP_DEBUG=false`, `APP_ENV=production` | `sudo cipi app env shop --get=APP_DEBUG` |
| Dependencies without known CVEs | `composer audit` in CI; [Checkpoint](https://checkpoint.web.ap.it/) for a broader Laravel audit |
| Secrets only in `.env`, never committed | `cipi.yml` lists required names (`env.required`), never values |
| Rate limiting on login, API and forms | `RateLimiter::for(...)` and the `throttle` middleware |
| Authorization on every route | Policies and gates; test them |
| Mass-assignment guarded | `$fillable` on models |
| Uploads validated and stored outside `public/` | `mimes:` rules, `Storage::disk('local')` |
| Admin tools (Horizon, Telescope, Pulse) gated | `viewHorizon` gate; Telescope off in production |
| Security headers | CSP, HSTS (after HTTPS works everywhere), `X-Frame-Options` |

## The server

| Check | Cipi does it with |
| --- | --- |
| Each app isolated from the others | Own Linux user, PHP pool with `open_basedir`, database user |
| SSH by key only, no root login | Installer default; `sudo cipi ssh list` |
| Firewall with only 22, 80, 443 | UFW by default; `sudo cipi firewall list` |
| Brute-force bans | fail2ban; `sudo cipi firewall attempts 3`; optional [CrowdSec](https://cipi.sh/docs/crowdsec) |
| PHP patched the day fixes ship | Nightly at 03:30; `sudo cipi php upgrade` ([case study](https://cipi.sh/guides/php-nginx-cve-patching)) |
| nginx patched | `sudo cipi nginx security`, `sudo cipi autoupdate on nginx` |
