| Credentials encrypted at rest | The vault (AES-256) for configs, tokens and keys |
| HTTPS everywhere | `sudo cipi ssl install shop` and `sudo cipi ssl force shop` |
| Malware and integrity checks | `sudo cipi scan`, nightly integrity checks |
| Compliance report | `sudo cipi compliance` |

## Access

| Check | How |
| --- | --- |
| Per-person SSH keys, removed when people leave | `sudo cipi ssh add`, `sudo cipi ssh remove` |
| Panel with 2FA or SSO, least-privilege roles | [Web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui-sso) |
| API tokens scoped and expiring | `cipi api token create --abilities=… --expires=…` |
| Staging and admin behind a login | [Cloudflare Access](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel) or basic auth |

## Data

| Check | How |
| --- | --- |
| Encrypted off-site backups, restored at least once | [Backups to S3](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3) with `encrypt: true` and `cipi backup verify` |
| No production data on laptops | [Anonymized dumps](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps) |
| Logs that expire | [Log retention](https://cipi.sh/docs/log-retention) |

## Monitoring

| Check | How |
| --- | --- |
| Alerts where you look | Telegram, Slack, e-mail or webhooks ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts)) |
| Health check with automatic rollback | `health.rollback_on_unhealthy: true` in `cipi.yml` |
| Who deployed what | The [deploy audit](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit) |


## How Cipi handled the November 2026 PHP and nginx CVEs

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/php-nginx-cve-patching

Two security releases landed within a day of each other in November 2026: **nginx 1.31.9** (18 November, ten CVEs) and a **PHP security release** for every supported branch (19 November). This is what reached a server running Cipi, what didn't, and why.

## nginx 1.31.9

| CVE | What | On a Cipi server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CVE-2026-118899 | Endless loop reading a request body over TLS 1.3: one request pins a worker at 100% CPU | **Reachable** on every HTTPS vhost. Fixed by the upgrade |
| CVE-2026-125283 | Buffer overflow with `try_files` under an `alias` | The panel API vhost had that pattern for `/api-docs`; the line is removed by the migration |
| CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633 | Memory corruption in HTTP/2 | **Not reachable**: Cipi writes `listen 443 ssl;` and never enables HTTP/2 |
| Six more | Resolver, HTTP/3, mail, stream, PROXY protocol v2 | Not used by Cipi |

What `cipi self-update` did:

```flow
Check | nginx -t passes on the current config
Simulate | one apt transaction, all or nothing
Upgrade | nginx.org mainline 1.31.9
Verify | the running binary is the new one
```

Servers installed between June and November 2026 were found on Ubuntu's archive nginx, which wasn't receiving these fixes. The migration moved them to nginx.org's mainline repository in one simulated transaction: if apt couldn't do all of it, nothing changed. When a long-lived WebSocket kept a worker on the old binary, Cipi restarted nginx instead of reloading (well under a second).

```bash
$ sudo cipi nginx security      # version vs fixes, running binary, any HTTP/2 config
$ dpkg-query -W nginx           # 1.31.9-1~noble = nginx.org
```

## PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and 8.6.0

| CVE | What | On a Cipi server before the update |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CVE-2026-129289 | Request smuggling in PHP-FPM | Needs `fastcgi_keep_conn`, which Cipi vhosts never set |
| CVE-2026-129291 | Use-after-free in the FPM master | Needs `catch_workers_output`, set only in the panel's own pools, plus code already running as that user |
| CVE-2026-126714, CVE-2026-115560 | Code execution through session files | Upload progress is off in every pool (admin flag): the upload path is closed |
| CVE-2026-129474 | Use-after-free in fatal-error backtraces (8.5+) | `fatal_error_backtraces` off in every pool |
| CVE-2026-129496 | Use-after-free of the timezone cache | **No setting closes it**: needs the update |

Hardening Cipi had already applied, as admin flags `.user.ini` and `ini_set()` can't undo:

```ini
php_admin_flag[session.upload_progress.enabled] = off
php_admin_flag[fatal_error_backtraces] = off
```

The fix itself:

```bash
$ sudo cipi php upgrade
```

Cipi installs PHP from packages.sury.org first, the fastest source for security releases, and patches **every night at 03:30**. While a version is `VULNERABLE`, the command exits 1 and the nightly job alerts until it's fixed. Only the affected FPM services restart.

## Octane apps

An Octane app runs the PHP compiled into its FrankenPHP binary. `cipi php upgrade` lists it as vulnerable until it runs a build with a fixed PHP:

```bash
$ sudo cipi frankenphp upgrade --all
```

If Octane doesn't answer after the upgrade, the previous build returns automatically.

## Lessons for any PHP server

| Practice | Why it mattered here |
| --- | --- |
| Don't enable features you don't need (HTTP/2 on a plain app vhost, keep-alive to FPM, upload progress) | Five CVEs needed one of them |
| Patch PHP from a source that ships fixes the same day | One CVE had no workaround |
| Alert while a known-vulnerable build is installed | Nobody has to remember to check |
| Treat embedded runtimes (FrankenPHP, Docker images) as separate patch targets | apt doesn't see them |

Follow security notes as they ship on the [Telegram channel](https://t.me/cipicloud).


## Back up Laravel apps and databases to S3, and restore them

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3

A backup you haven't restored is a hope. This guide sets up encrypted backups to S3-compatible storage, checks them automatically and walks through a restore.

```flow
Destination | S3-compatible bucket
Profiles | what, how often, how long
Run | scheduled, encrypted
Verify | archives readable
Restore | one app or everything
```

## 1. Add a destination

Create a bucket and an access key limited to it, at any S3-compatible provider. Then:

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup configure                 # interactive: endpoint, bucket, keys
$ sudo cipi backup destination test
```

Secret keys are entered on the server and never travel through the panel or the API.

## 2. Create profiles

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup profile add nightly --scope=all --cron='0 2 * * *' --keep-days=14 \
    --dest=s3 --encrypt
$ sudo cipi backup profile add hourly-db --scope=db --databases='shop,tenant_*' \
    --exclude-tables='*.jobs,*.telescope_*' --every=30m --keep=48 --dest=local
$ sudo cipi backup status
```

| Scope | Contains |
| --- | --- |
| `db` | Database dumps |
| `files` | Each app's `shared/` (`.env`, `storage`, uploads) |
| `all` | Both |

`cipi backup status` flags apps and databases that **no enabled profile covers**, so a new app can't silently go unprotected.

## 3. Let the app declare its own backups

```yaml
# cipi.yml
backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: shop-db, scope: db, every: 30m, keep: 48, destinations: [local] }
    - { name: shop-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 2 * * *", keep_days: 14, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

Profile names must start with the app's name, so a repository can't touch another app's backups.

## 4. Verify

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup verify           # archives present and readable
$ sudo cipi backup verify --deep    # also decrypts and checks contents
```

Failures go to your [notification channels](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts).

## 5. Restore

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup list --profile=nightly
$ sudo cipi backup fetch nightly 2026-11-22_020000 --dest=/root/restore
$ sudo cipi db restore shop /root/restore/shop.sql.gz
```

For a whole server, restoring backups works, but moving with [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) is faster when the old server is still alive.

## Before risky deploys

A local snapshot before migrations is cheap: `sudo cipi app edit shop --predeploy-snapshot`. See [safe migrations](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-zero-downtime-migrations).


## The Cipi web panel and REST API

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-gui-and-api

Cipi is CLI-first, but not CLI-only. Two optional pieces, each on its own subdomain, open it up: the **API** (for automation, the panel, the CLI client and AI assistants) and the **web panel** (for people).

```stack
Browser, cipi-cli, SDK, MCP | clients
Cipi API | api.example.com, token per client
cipi CLI | same code path as SSH
```

## 1. Install the API

```bash
$ sudo cipi api api.example.com
$ sudo cipi api token create --name=panel --full-access
```

The API checks DNS, issues its certificate and runs as `www-data`, calling an allowlist of `cipi` commands. Installing software or dropping data stays on the CLI.

## 2. Install the panel

```bash
$ sudo cipi gui panel.example.com
```

Log in with the admin account it asks for, then **Connections → add server** with the API URL and token. Add more servers the same way: the panel shows them as one fleet.

## 3. Invite the team

| Role | Sees |
| --- | --- |
| Admin | Everything |
| User | Only granted servers (View or Manage) or apps (View, Deploy, Edit, Environment, Logs, Commands, Delete) |

Invites are copyable links that work once and expire after seven days. Turn on TOTP 2FA per user, or [single sign-on](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui-sso) with Entra ID, Google Workspace, Okta or any OIDC provider.

## 4. Automate with the API

```bash
$ cipi-cli api token add prod      # on your laptop
$ cipi-cli prod apps list
$ cipi-cli prod deploy shop
```

Or from PHP with the [SDK](https://cipi.sh/docs/php-sdk), from WHMCS with the [module](https://cipi.sh/docs/whmcs), or from an assistant with the [MCP server](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents).

## 5. Lock it down

| Step | How |
| --- | --- |
| IP allowlist for the API | `sudo cipi api ip-whitelist set --ips=203.0.113.0/24` |
| Panel behind Cloudflare Access | `sudo cipi zt access enable --gui` ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel)) |
| Small tokens | One per client, only the abilities it needs, with an expiry |
| Keep it current | `sudo cipi gui update`, `sudo cipi api update` (the API also updates nightly) |


## Move Laravel apps to a new server with cipi sync

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync

`cipi sync` copies whole apps between Cipi servers: configuration, deploy keys, workers, crontab, PHP version and, if you want, database and storage. Archives are encrypted with AES-256. The old server keeps serving until you switch DNS.

## 1. Prepare the new server

Install Cipi on it ([providers](https://cipi.sh/guides/#providers)) and install the same PHP versions your apps use (`sudo cipi php install 8.5`).

## 2. Trust between the two servers

```bash
# old server
$ sudo cipi sync pubkey
# new server: paste it
$ sudo cipi sync trust
```

## 3. Push the apps

```bash
$ sudo cipi sync push --host=203.0.113.20 --with-db --with-storage --import
```

Or one app at a time: `sudo cipi sync push shop --host=…`.

| Travels | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| `.env`, `auth.json`, `deploy.php` | Always |
| Deploy key and SSH config | The same key keeps working on GitHub |
| Workers, crontab, PHP version, limits | Always |
| Database | With `--with-db`; new database password on a new app |
| `shared/storage` | With `--with-storage` |
| Certificates | Never: issued on the new server after DNS moves |

## 4. Test before switching

Point your laptop's `/etc/hosts` at the new IP and browse the app. Then deploy once on the new server to check the Git path end to end:

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop
```

## 5. Switch DNS, then certificates

Lower the TTL a day before. Change the `A` records, wait for propagation, then:

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop
```

Run a last `sync push --with-db --update` just before the switch if the database changed in the meantime.

## Keep a warm standby

The same command on a schedule replicates apps to a second server. Combined with [backups](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3), it covers both "restore yesterday" and "this server is gone".


## Server monitoring and alerts on Telegram, Slack and e-mail

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts

Cipi checks the server every five minutes with a cron job and a few state files: no agent, no metrics database, no external service. You choose where the alerts go.

## 1. Add a channel

```bash
$ sudo cipi notification add telegram oncall --token= --chat-id=
$ sudo cipi notification add slack ops --url=https://hooks.slack.com/services/…
$ sudo cipi notification add webhook pager --url=https://example.com/hooks/cipi --secret=…
$ sudo cipi notification test all
```

For Telegram: create a bot with @BotFather, send it `/start`, and read the chat id from `getUpdates`. Group chats have negative ids.

## 2. Pick what notifies

```bash
$ sudo cipi notification triggers
$ sudo cipi notification triggers disable monitor_load
```

Deploy failures, backups, health checks, monitor alerts, security events and SSO changes are separate triggers.

## 3. Tune the monitor

```bash
$ sudo cipi monitor list
$ sudo cipi monitor set disk --warn=85 --crit=95
$ sudo cipi monitor test
```

| Check | Alerts on |
| --- | --- |
| CPU, load, memory, swap | Sustained high usage |
| Disk | Thresholds per filesystem; [`cipi disk`](https://cipi.sh/docs/disk) shows which app is filling it |
| Services | nginx, databases, Valkey, Supervisor, PHP-FPM down |
| Certificates | Expiring soon |
| App disk | An app over its soft limit |

## 4. Watch each app from outside

```bash
$ sudo cipi health set shop --url=https://shop.example.com/up --expect=200
$ sudo cipi health check shop
```

The same check runs after every deploy and can [roll back automatically](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-zero-downtime-migrations). For a richer per-app status (database, cache, queue, storage, deploy), use the [agent's health endpoint](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-health-monitoring) with an external uptime service.


## Deploy a Symfony app on an Ubuntu VPS with Cipi

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-symfony

Cipi is Laravel-first, but any PHP framework runs as a **custom app**: Nginx serves the document root you pick, PHP-FPM runs in the app's own pool, and Git deploys pull into `~/htdocs`. Here's a Symfony app end to end.

## 1. Create the app and the database

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --custom --user=billing --domain=billing.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/billing.git --branch=main --docroot=public --php=8.4
$ sudo cipi db create --name=billing                 # or --engine=pgsql
```

Add the deploy key from the summary to the repository (read-only).

## 2. Configure the environment

As the app user, create `~/htdocs/.env.local` (never committed):

```bash
APP_ENV=prod
APP_SECRET=change-me
DATABASE_URL="mysql://billing:PASSWORD@127.0.0.1:3306/billing?serverVersion=mariadb-11.4.0"
```

## 3. Build after every deploy

Custom apps pull the code; `cipi.yml` runs the build steps from the live folder:

```yaml
# cipi.yml
version: 1
deploy:
  post:
    - composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader --no-interaction
    - php bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate --no-interaction
    - php bin/console cache:clear
  post_on_failure: abort
```

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy billing
```

> [!note] Custom apps deploy in place (a pull into `htdocs`), not as atomic releases like Laravel apps. Keep migrations backward compatible and deploy at quiet times, or put the app behind [Cloudflare](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel) with a maintenance page.

## 4. Messenger and scheduled tasks

As the app user (`crontab -e`):

```text
* * * * * php ~/htdocs/bin/console messenger:consume async --time-limit=55 --quiet
```

Each run consumes for 55 seconds and exits, so a deploy never leaves an old worker running for long.

## 5. HTTPS, backups, alerts

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install billing
$ sudo cipi backup profile add billing-nightly --scope=all --cron='0 2 * * *' --keep-days=14 --dest=s3 --encrypt
$ sudo cipi health set billing --url=https://billing.example.com/ --expect=200
```

Everything else (firewall, PHP patches, monitoring) is server-wide and already on.


## Host WordPress on your own VPS next to Laravel apps

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-wordpress-custom-app

WordPress isn't Laravel, but it's PHP, and Cipi hosts it as a **custom app**: its own user, PHP pool, Nginx vhost and certificate, isolated from everything else on the server.

| | Laravel app | Custom app (WordPress) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code | Zero-downtime releases | `~/htdocs`, from Git or SFTP |
| Database | Created | One command |
| Workers, scheduler | Yes | Use the app user's crontab |

## 1. Create the app and its database

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --custom --user=blog --domain=blog.example.com
$ sudo cipi db create --name=blog
```

Save the database password from the output. For a site in Git (a theme or Bedrock), add `--repository=git@github.com:acme/blog.git` and, with Bedrock, `--docroot=web`.

## 2. Upload WordPress

SFTP as the app user to `~/htdocs` (the credentials are in the create summary), or from SSH:

```bash
$ ssh blog@203.0.113.10
$ cd ~/htdocs && rm -f index.html
$ curl -sO https://wordpress.org/latest.tar.gz && tar xzf latest.tar.gz --strip-components=1 && rm latest.tar.gz
```

Open `https://blog.example.com` (after step 3) and run the installer with database `blog`, user `blog` and the saved password, host `127.0.0.1`.

## 3. HTTPS

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install blog
$ sudo cipi ssl force blog
```

Set both URLs to `https://` in **Settings → General**.

## 4. Real cron instead of WP-Cron

In `wp-config.php`: `define('DISABLE_WP_CRON', true);` then, as the app user (`crontab -e`):

```text
*/5 * * * * php ~/htdocs/wp-cron.php >/dev/null 2>&1
```

## 5. PHP settings and limits

```yaml
# cipi.yml in htdocs (vhosts never serve it)
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.4"
  ini: { upload_max_filesize: 64M, post_max_size: 64M, memory_limit: 256M }
```

Or from the CLI: `sudo cipi app edit blog --php=8.4`. Check plugin compatibility before moving to a newer PHP.

## 6. Back it up

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup profile add blog-nightly --scope=all --cron='0 3 * * *' --keep-days=14 --dest=s3 --encrypt
```

`all` covers the database and the files. More in [backups to S3](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3). Running a shop? See [WooCommerce on a VPS](https://cipi.sh/guides/woocommerce-vps).


## Self-host PHP e-commerce (PrestaShop, Sylius, Bagisto and more) on a VPS

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/php-ecommerce-vps

PHP runs a large part of online commerce. Here's how the main open-source platforms map onto a Cipi server: Laravel-based ones run as Laravel apps with zero-downtime deploys, the rest as custom apps.

| Platform | Built on | Run on Cipi as | Document root | Extra services |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Bagisto** | Laravel | Laravel app | (managed) | Queue, scheduler: built in |
| **Lunar** | Laravel package | Laravel app | (managed) | Search via [Meilisearch](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-scout-meilisearch) |
| **Aimeos** | Laravel package | Laravel app | (managed) | Queue, scheduler |
| **Sylius** | Symfony | Custom app | `public` | Messenger via cron ([Symfony guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-symfony)) |
| **PrestaShop** | Symfony + legacy | Custom app | root | Cron for modules |
| **WooCommerce** | WordPress | Custom app | root | [Real cron](https://cipi.sh/guides/woocommerce-vps) |
| **Magento / Adobe Commerce** | Laminas/Symfony | Possible as custom app | `pub` | Needs OpenSearch, which Cipi doesn't install: host it elsewhere |

## Laravel-based shops (Bagisto, Lunar, Aimeos)

They get everything Laravel apps get: atomic releases, workers, scheduler, `cipi.yml`, health checks with rollback.

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=store --domain=store.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/store.git --php=8.4
$ sudo cipi deploy store && sudo cipi ssl install store
```

## Custom-app shops (PrestaShop, Sylius)

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --custom --user=store --domain=store.example.com --docroot=public   # Sylius
$ sudo cipi db create --name=store
```

Then follow the platform's installer. Build steps after each Git deploy go in `cipi.yml` `deploy.post` (Composer, migrations, cache), as in the [Symfony guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-symfony).

## What every shop should set

| Need | Command |
| --- | --- |
| HTTPS, forced | `sudo cipi ssl install store && sudo cipi ssl force store` |
| Frequent database backups | A `--every=30m` profile plus a nightly encrypted one to S3 ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3)) |
| PHP limits | `app.ini` in `cipi.yml`: `memory_limit`, `max_execution_time`, upload sizes |
| Enough PHP workers | `sudo cipi app limits store --fpm-max-children=12` |
| A staging copy | Laravel shops: `sudo cipi app clone store --name=store-stg --domain=… --env=staging`; others: a second custom app with a restored dump |
| Alerts | [Telegram, Slack or e-mail](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts) |

> [!note] Check each platform's PHP version support before you pick a version per app. Cipi runs several PHP versions side by side, so a shop on PHP 8.3 and another on 8.5 can share a server.


## WooCommerce on your own VPS: fast, isolated and backed up

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/woocommerce-vps

A shop has stricter needs than a blog: orders arrive all day, so backups must be frequent, cron must be real, and updates must be tried somewhere safe first. Start from [WordPress on a VPS](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-wordpress-custom-app), then add the steps below.

## 1. Size the server

| Shop | Starting point |
| --- | --- |
| Small catalogue, few orders a day | 2 GB RAM |
| Thousands of products, steady traffic | 4 GB+ RAM, more PHP workers |

```bash
$ sudo cipi app limits shop --fpm-max-children=12
```

## 2. PHP limits for imports and big carts

```yaml
# cipi.yml in htdocs
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.4"
  ini: { memory_limit: 512M, max_execution_time: 120, upload_max_filesize: 64M, post_max_size: 64M }
```

## 3. Real cron

WooCommerce schedules emails, stock holds and webhooks through Action Scheduler. With `DISABLE_WP_CRON` set to true in `wp-config.php`, run it every minute as the app user:

```text
* * * * * php ~/htdocs/wp-cron.php >/dev/null 2>&1
```

## 4. Backups that match your orders

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup profile add shop-db --scope=db --databases=shop --every=30m --keep=48 --dest=local
$ sudo cipi backup profile add shop-nightly --scope=all --cron='0 3 * * *' --keep-days=30 --dest=s3 --encrypt
$ sudo cipi backup verify
```

Half-hourly database dumps limit what you could lose to thirty minutes of orders.

## 5. A staging copy for updates

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --custom --user=shopstg --domain=staging.shop.example.com
$ sudo cipi db create --name=shopstg
$ sudo cipi basicauth enable shopstg
```

Copy the files (`rsync` between the two `htdocs` as root) and restore last night's dump into `shopstg`, then point `wp-config.php` and the site URLs at staging. Update plugins and themes there first. Turn off payment webhooks and outgoing e-mail on staging.

## 6. Security basics

| Item | How |
| --- | --- |
| HTTPS everywhere | `sudo cipi ssl install shop && sudo cipi ssl force shop` |
| Admin brute force | fail2ban is on; add Cloudflare Access on `/wp-admin` if you can ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel)) |
| Malware | `sudo cipi scan shop` |
| PHP patched | Nightly, automatically |

# Comparisons


## Cipi vs 20i

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-20i

## At a glance 

| | Cipi | 20i |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model | Software on your VPS | Hosting plans, reseller, domains, e-mail |
| Price | Free tool; fixed VPS price | Hosting plans |
| Laravel deploys | Zero-downtime releases, workers, Octane | Managed hosting |
| Support | Community | In-house support |

## Where they differ 

Different categories. Pick 20i for a hosting business; pick Cipi to run your own apps on your own servers.

## Moving to Cipi 

```flow
New VPS | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04
Install | one command
Create apps | same repos, same domains
Copy data | database dump and storage
Switch DNS | then issue certificates
```

Install Cipi on a fresh server, recreate each app with `cipi app create` (same repository and domain), import the database with `cipi db restore`, copy `storage/`, deploy, then move DNS and run `cipi ssl install`. Already on Cipi elsewhere? [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) moves apps between servers in one command.


## The best Laravel Forge alternatives in 2026

URL: https://cipi.sh/best-laravel-forge-alternatives

Forge made deploying Laravel to your own server easy. It's also a subscription, and the control plane lives on someone else's servers. Here are the alternatives, grouped by how they work.

| Tool | Model | Price | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Cipi** | Self-hosted, CLI + optional panel | Free (MIT) | Laravel teams that want everything on their own server, configuration in Git and AI tooling |
| Vito Deploy | Self-hosted dashboard | Free | Teams that want a central, plugin-friendly GUI |
| Ploi | SaaS panel | Free tier, then €8–30/month by server count | A Forge-like hosted panel based in the EU |
| RunCloud, Cleavr | SaaS panels | Paid plans | Hosted GUI, PHP and WordPress-friendly |
| Laravel Cloud | Managed platform | From $5/month plus usage | No servers, autoscaling |
| Coolify | Self-hosted Docker platform | Free | Containers for many stacks |
| Kamal | Deploy tool | Free | Docker teams that provision servers themselves |

## 1. Cipi

Free and open source. One command turns an Ubuntu VPS into a hardened Laravel platform: zero-downtime releases, workers, scheduler, Octane, Horizon, Reverb, Meilisearch, backups to S3, monitoring and nightly security patches. Server settings can live in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml); the [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) and [API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) are optional and self-hosted; [MCP servers](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents) let AI assistants help safely. [Cipi vs Forge](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-laravel-forge).

## 2. Vito Deploy

Free, open-source dashboard built with Laravel, with provider integrations, plugins and workflows. Runs as its own app that manages your servers. [Cipi vs Vito Deploy](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-vito-deploy).

## 3. Ploi

The closest SaaS to Forge, from the Netherlands, with plans by server count and an MCP server. [Cipi vs Ploi](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-ploi).

## 4. RunCloud and Cleavr

Hosted panels with PHP and WordPress strengths. [RunCloud](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-runcloud), [Cleavr](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-cleavr).

## 5. Laravel Cloud

No servers: you push code and pay usage, with autoscaling and scale-to-zero. [Cipi vs Laravel Cloud](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-laravel-cloud).

## 6. Coolify

A self-hosted Docker platform for any stack. [Cipi vs Coolify](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-coolify).

## 7. Kamal

Container deploys over SSH to servers you prepare. [Cipi vs Kamal](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-kamal).

## How to choose

```flow
Want to own the server? | no → Laravel Cloud
Laravel or PHP? | many stacks → Coolify
Want a subscription? | yes → Ploi or Forge
Otherwise | Cipi or Vito Deploy
```


## Cipi vs Cleavr

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-cleavr

## At a glance 

| | Cipi | Cleavr |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free | Paid plans |
| Where it runs | On your own VPS; no external control plane | Cleavr SaaS |
| Zero-downtime deploys | Yes | Yes |
| Web dashboard | Optional, self-hosted | Yes |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | No |
| AI assistants (MCP) | Built in | Not advertised |
| Encrypted credentials at rest | Vault (AES-256) | Not advertised |

## Where they differ 

Both deploy Laravel with zero downtime. Cleavr keeps the control plane in its SaaS; Cipi keeps it on each server and adds a self-hosted [panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) only if you want one.

## Moving to Cipi 

```flow
New VPS | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04
Install | one command
Create apps | same repos, same domains
Copy data | database dump and storage
Switch DNS | then issue certificates
```

Install Cipi on a fresh server, recreate each app with `cipi app create` (same repository and domain), import the database with `cipi db restore`, copy `storage/`, deploy, then move DNS and run `cipi ssl install`. Already on Cipi elsewhere? [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) moves apps between servers in one command.


## Cipi vs CloudPanel

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-cloudpanel

## At a glance 

| | Cipi | CloudPanel |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free (MIT) | Free |
| Interface | CLI, optional panel, API | Web GUI and CLI |
| Focus | Laravel-first, PHP and Node apps | PHP, Node.js, Python, static |
| Laravel releases, workers, scheduler | Built in | Manual |
| Zero-downtime Git deploys | Yes | No built-in release system |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | No |
| AI assistants (MCP) | Built in | Not advertised |

## Where they differ 

CloudPanel is a good generic panel. Cipi knows Laravel: releases, `.env`, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb and Octane are handled for you.

## Moving to Cipi 

```flow
New VPS | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04
Install | one command
Create apps | same repos, same domains
Copy data | database dump and storage
Switch DNS | then issue certificates
```

Install Cipi on a fresh server, recreate each app with `cipi app create` (same repository and domain), import the database with `cipi db restore`, copy `storage/`, deploy, then move DNS and run `cipi ssl install`. Already on Cipi elsewhere? [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) moves apps between servers in one command.


## Cipi vs Coolify

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-coolify

## At a glance 

| | Cipi | Coolify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free (MIT) | Free (self-hosted) |
| Model | Native Nginx, PHP-FPM or Octane, databases on Ubuntu | Docker containers behind a proxy |
| Interface | CLI first, optional panel | Web dashboard |
| Laravel lifecycle | Releases, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb built in | Generic app containers |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | Compose files and dashboard settings |
| AI assistants (MCP) | Built in | Not advertised |
| One-click services | Meilisearch, PostgreSQL, Valkey | Large catalogue |

## Where they differ 

Coolify is excellent when you think in containers and host many stacks. Cipi removes the container layer for PHP: less overhead, simpler debugging, and Laravel's lifecycle built in.

## Moving to Cipi 

```flow
New VPS | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04
Install | one command
Create apps | same repos, same domains
Copy data | database dump and storage
Switch DNS | then issue certificates
```

Install Cipi on a fresh server, recreate each app with `cipi app create` (same repository and domain), import the database with `cipi db restore`, copy `storage/`, deploy, then move DNS and run `cipi ssl install`. Already on Cipi elsewhere? [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) moves apps between servers in one command.

## Cipi vs Laravel Cloud

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-laravel-cloud

## At a glance 

| | Cipi | Laravel Cloud |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pricing | Free tool; fixed VPS price | Plans from $5/month plus usage |
| Servers | Your VPS, full root | None to manage, no root |
| Autoscaling, scale-to-zero | No: size the VPS | Yes |
| Managed databases and cache | On your VPS (MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Valkey) | Managed |
| Octane, queues, Reverb | Yes | Yes |
| Portability | Standard Ubuntu stack, any provider | Tied to the platform |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | Environment settings in the platform |

## Where they differ 

This is a choice of model rather than features. Laravel Cloud hides servers and bills what you use: ideal for spiky traffic and teams that never want to administer anything. Cipi gives you a server you own, at a fixed price, with the automation a platform would give you: zero-downtime deploys, workers, backups, patching and alerts.

## Cipi vs Laravel Forge

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-laravel-forge

## At a glance 

| | Cipi | Laravel Forge |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free | Hobby $12, Growth $19, Business $39 per month (account plans) |
| Where it runs | On your own VPS; no external control plane | forge.laravel.com (SaaS) |
| Server provisioning on clouds | You create the VPS; Cipi installs everything | Creates servers on major clouds and on Laravel VPS |
| Zero-downtime deploys | Yes, atomic releases with rollback | Yes |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml`, planned and applied | Deploy script in the dashboard |
| Web dashboard | Optional, self-hosted, multi-server, roles and SSO | Yes, hosted |
| CLI and API | Full CLI, REST API, cipi-cli, PHP SDK | API and CLI |
| AI assistants (MCP) | Two built-in MCP servers | Community MCP servers via the API |
| Security patching | PHP nightly, nginx via autoupdate, alerts while vulnerable | Server packages via unattended upgrades |
| Deploy audit trail | Hash-chained ledger of every deploy | Deployment history |
| Your infrastructure data | Stays on your server | Stored by a US-based SaaS |

## Where they differ 

**Where the control plane lives.** Forge manages your servers from its own SaaS. Cipi is installed on each server: there's no account to keep paying, and nothing breaks if a third party is down. The optional [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) is also self-hosted.

**Configuration as code.** With Cipi, PHP version, workers, scheduler, domains, health checks and backups can live in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml) and change through a pull request, with a plan before anything is applied.

**Safety by default.** Each app gets its own Linux user, PHP pool and database user. PHP is patched every night from the fastest source and the server alerts while a known-vulnerable build is installed ([case study](https://cipi.sh/guides/php-nginx-cve-patching)).

**Where Forge wins.** Server creation on cloud providers, Laravel VPS, a mature hosted dashboard and the backing of the Laravel team.

## Moving to Cipi 

```flow
New VPS | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04
Install | one command
Create apps | same repos, same domains
Copy data | database dump and storage
Switch DNS | then issue certificates
```

Install Cipi on a fresh server, recreate each app with `cipi app create` (same repository and domain), import the database with `cipi db restore`, copy `storage/`, deploy, then move DNS and run `cipi ssl install`. Already on Cipi elsewhere? [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) moves apps between servers in one command.

Cipi gives you the same day-to-day jobs (deploys, queues, SSL, databases, backups, monitoring) with no plan at all, because it runs on the server you already pay for.

The trade-off is creation: Ploi can create servers at your cloud provider; with Cipi you create the VPS and run one command. Not to be confused with [Ploi Cloud](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-ploi-cloud), a separate PaaS.

## Cipi vs Vito Deploy

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-vito-deploy

## At a glance 

| | Cipi | Vito Deploy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free (MIT) | Free, open source |
| Architecture | Installed on each server; optional panel manages many | A Laravel app on its own server that manages others over SSH |
| Interface | CLI first, optional panel, API, cipi-cli, SDK | Web dashboard and API |
| Server creation on clouds | You create the VPS | Provider integrations and workflows |
| Zero-downtime Laravel deploys | Atomic releases, rollback, health-checked | Deployment scripts |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | Dashboard settings |
| Extensibility | `deploy.post`, Deployer tasks, API | Plugins and workflows |
| AI assistants (MCP) | Two built-in MCP servers | Not advertised |
| Security patching | Nightly PHP, nginx autoupdate, alerts while vulnerable | Not advertised |
| Encrypted credentials at rest | Vault (AES-256) | Not advertised |

## Where they differ 

Vito and Cipi share a philosophy: free, open source, no SaaS. The architecture differs. Vito is a central dashboard (a Laravel app with its own database) that provisions and manages servers. Cipi is installed on each server and works without any dashboard; its [optional panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) talks to each server's API when you want a browser view of the fleet.

Cipi goes deeper on running Laravel in production: atomic releases with health-checked rollback, Octane and Reverb wiring, [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml), a deploy audit ledger, MCP servers, and security patching with alerts. Vito shines with plugins and workflows.

# cipi.yml: your server settings, in your repository

URL: https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml

Edit cipi.ymlin a branch
Reviewin the pull request
Deploythe file ships with the release
Planevery change listed
Applyall or nothing

## 1. Edit: the whole app, in one file 

```yaml
version: 1

app:
  php: "8.6"
  aliases: ["www.shop.example.com"]
  www: to-root
  ini: { upload_max_filesize: 50M }

workers:
  horizon: true
  reverb: true

schedule: true
search: true

health:
  url: "https://shop.example.com/up"
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true

deploy:
  predeploy_snapshot: true
  node_build: "npm ci && npm run build"
  post:
    - artisan scout:sync-index-settings

env: { required: [STRIPE_KEY, MAIL_HOST] }

backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: shop-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 2 * * *", keep_days: 14, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

| Block | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| `app` | PHP version, aliases, www/apex, `php.ini` values, resource limits, basic auth |
| `workers`, `schedule` | Queues, Horizon, Reverb, the scheduler |
| `search` | Meilisearch for Laravel Scout |
| `health` | URL probed every 5 minutes and after each deploy, with automatic rollback |
| `deploy` | Branch, releases kept, DB snapshot, asset build, post-deploy steps |
| `databases`, `backup` | Extra databases and backup profiles for this app |
| `redirects`, `proxies`, `crons`, `node` | Routes, scheduled commands, Node apps |

Full reference: [cipi.yml docs](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml). Ready-made files: [recipes](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-recipes).

## 2. Review: validate before you push 

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent
$ php artisan cipi:yml validate          # same validator as the server
$ php artisan cipi:yml generate --write  # a first file inferred from your code
$ php artisan cipi:yml schema --write    # autocompletion in your editor
```

Add `php artisan cipi:yml validate --json` to CI and a broken file never reaches a server. AI assistants connected through the [agent's MCP](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents) can validate drafts too.

## 3. Deploy: one repository, every environment 

The file ships inside each release: what you merged is what the server reads. Which file an app reads depends on its environment.

| File | Read by |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi.yml` | Production apps |
| `cipi-staging.yml` | Apps created with `--env=staging` |
| `cipi-preview.yml` | Preview apps per branch |

Walkthrough: [staging and production from one repository](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-staging-production).

## 4. Plan: see every change first 

`plan` lists each change and each blocker. `apply` performs them in one transaction. `auto on` applies the file after every successful deploy, from the CLI, the webhook or the panel.

## 5. Apply: all or nothing, safe to accept from Git 

`cipi yml apply` performs the plan in one transaction: if any step fails, nothing is left half done. With `cipi yml auto  on` it runs after every deploy. Anyone who can push controls the file, so it's designed to fail closed.

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Configure only | It can never create, rename or delete an app |
| Namespaced | Databases are `shop` or `shop_*`, backup profiles `shop` or `shop-*`: no reaching into other apps |
| No secrets | Required variables are names; generated credentials stay on the server |
| No shell | Only allowlisted runners (`artisan`, `composer`, `npm`, `php`…), no pipes or `;` |
| Small YAML | Anchors, tags, merges and block scalars are refused |
| Strict routes | Proxies can't target Cipi's own ports, link-local or cloud-metadata addresses |
| Server picks the file | Staging reads `cipi-staging.yml` because the server says so, never because a commit asks |

## Start in two minutes 

```bash
$ sudo cipi yml generate shop --save      # the app as it is today
$ cat /home/shop/cipi.yml                 # commit it at the repository root
$ sudo cipi deploy shop && sudo cipi yml plan shop
```

Step by step: [keep your server settings in the repository](https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml).
